title: Trading & market fundamentals
description: Your first course: understand stocks, markets, orders, returns, and risk before exploring investment strategies.

modules.title: What investing and trading mean
modules.subtitle: Start with goals, time horizons, and uncertainty
modules.objective: Distinguish saving, investing, and trading; calculate a simple return and explain why a profit is uncertain.
modules.content:
## The idea

Saving sets money aside for future use. Investing commits capital to an asset with an uncertain future payoff. Trading buys and sells assets in an attempt to benefit from price changes. Their boundaries overlap: an investor still trades when entering or leaving a position. The useful distinction is the purpose, holding period, and evidence behind the decision.

A long-term investor might study a business's ability to generate cash over years. A short-term trader might study an order imbalance over minutes. Neither time horizon guarantees success. Start by asking: **What am I buying, why might it pay me, when might I need the money, and how could I lose it?**

## A worked example

Maya spends $200 on a fictional investment and later receives $220 when she sells it. Ignoring costs and distributions, the gain is $20 and the return is $20 / $200 = 10%. If the sale brings $170 instead, the return is −15%. A hoped-for 10% return is an expectation, not money already earned.

$$R = \frac{\text{ending value} - \text{starting value}}{\text{starting value}}$$

Always state the time period. A 10% return over one month and a 10% return over five years are different outcomes. Compare investments over matching periods and account for costs before deciding which performed better.

## Build a decision before a position

Write a goal, a time horizon, a reason for the investment, and a condition that would invalidate that reason. Money needed soon has less time to recover from a fall. A promise of high returns with no risk is a reason to investigate the claim, not a substitute for evidence.

For this course, use hypothetical money. No brokerage account or coding experience is needed. Reading, arithmetic, and explaining your choices are enough. The optional Python example lets you change the numbers; its separate synthetic trading rule is not a recommended strategy.

## Connect to later courses

Graham & Dodd develops the distinction between price and estimated value. Statistical foundations teaches how to express uncertainty instead of treating a successful outcome as proof of skill.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Stocks, shares, and business ownership
modules.subtitle: Understand what a stockholder actually owns
modules.objective: Explain equity ownership, market capitalization, dividends, and why share price alone does not measure value.
modules.content:
## The idea

A share of stock is an ownership interest in a company. Common equity is a residual claim: creditors and other senior claims come first. Owners can benefit from price appreciation and dividends, but dividends are not automatic and shareholders can lose their investment. Voting rights depend on the share class.

Separate three quantities: **share price** is the market price of one share; **shares outstanding** is the number issued and held; **market capitalization** is their product. Market capitalization describes the market value of equity, not the company's cash balance or an independent estimate of what the business is worth.

## A worked example

Fictional Harbor Foods has 1,000,000 shares outstanding at $20 each. Its equity market capitalization is $20 million. Owning 100 shares means owning 100 / 1,000,000 = 0.01% of that share class, worth $2,000 at the quote. A declared $0.50 dividend per share would pay $50 on those 100 shares before taxes.

$$\text{Market capitalization} = \text{price per share}\times\text{shares outstanding}$$

Another company has 100 million shares trading at $2, so its market capitalization is $200 million. Its lower share price does not make the entire business cheaper than Harbor Foods.

## Splits and dilution

In a two-for-one stock split, 100 shares become 200; a theoretical $20 price becomes $10. The split itself leaves the $2,000 position value and ownership fraction unchanged. Real market prices may also move that day. A new share issuance is different: if your share count stays fixed while total shares increase, your ownership percentage falls. The company may receive new capital in exchange.

A dividend is a distribution of company resources, not free additional wealth. All else equal, distributing cash reduces the company's value. Later return calculations include both price changes and cash distributions.

## Connect to later courses

Security analysis uses diluted shares and the priority of claims to calculate per-share value. Keep the denominator and the company-wide amounts consistent.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: How stock markets work
modules.subtitle: Meet issuers, investors, brokers, exchanges, and indexes
modules.objective: Trace a stock transaction and distinguish the primary market, secondary market, an index, and an ETF.
modules.content:
## The idea

In a primary-market offering, a company issues new securities to raise money. In the secondary market, existing securities change hands between investors. When you buy already-issued shares from another investor, your payment generally goes to that seller, not to the company.

A broker receives and routes your order. An exchange or other trading venue brings together buying and selling interest. Market makers quote prices at which they are willing to trade, subject to available size. Clearing and settlement handle the obligations after execution. A submitted order, a filled trade, and completed settlement are different stages.

Hours, settlement schedules, lot sizes, currencies, and account rules vary by market and broker. A lesson using dollar amounts does not imply those conventions apply to every exchange.

## A worked example

Harbor Foods issues 100,000 new shares at $20, raising $2 million before offering costs. Later, Maya buys 50 existing shares from Leo for $21 each through a broker. The $1,050 secondary-market payment goes to the selling side; Harbor Foods does not receive another $1,050 in capital from that trade.

## Indexes, funds, and asset classes

An index is a rules-based measure of a basket of assets. An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on a market; it may seek to track an index, pursue an active strategy, or hold a narrow exposure. You buy fund shares, not the abstract index number. Fees and tracking differences can separate fund returns from index returns.

| Instrument | Basic economic claim | A question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stock | Business ownership | Can the business create durable value? |
| Bond | A debt claim with contractual terms | Can the issuer meet its obligations? |
| Fund / ETF | An interest in a pooled portfolio | What does it hold, and what does it cost? |
| Derivative | A contract tied to an underlying variable | What payoff and obligations does the contract create? |

Owning several funds does not necessarily create different exposures: their largest holdings may overlap. Likewise, an index moving up does not mean every constituent rose.

## Connect to later courses

Factor models use benchmarks; portfolio courses examine the exposures inside funds; execution courses distinguish an order's intent from what actually fills.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Prices, quotes, and order types
modules.subtitle: Read a quote and understand the trade-off between price and execution
modules.objective: Calculate a spread, interpret OHLCV, and choose between market, limit, stop, and stop-limit orders in a hypothetical scenario.
modules.content:
## The idea

The **bid** is a quoted buying price and the **ask** a quoted selling price. Their difference is the spread. The last traded price is a past transaction, so it is not a promise of your next fill. Available quantity matters: a large order can consume several price levels.

OHLCV records the open, high, low, close, and traded volume for a period. A candle summarizes that period; it does not reveal the sequence of every trade. Volume is shares traded, not the number of distinct people buying.

## A worked example

A fictional quote shows bid $49.90 for 100 shares and ask $50.10 for 80 shares. The spread is $0.20. A small market buy may execute near $50.10; a market sell may execute near $49.90. An immediate buy and sell of 10 shares at those prices loses $2 before fees, even if the quotes do not change. A request for 200 shares cannot assume all 200 are available at the displayed ask.

$$\text{Spread}=\text{ask}-\text{bid}$$

## Translate an intention into an order

| Order | Instruction | Main trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market | Trade at available prices | Execution price is uncertain |
| Buy limit | Buy at the limit or lower | May fill partly or not at all |
| Sell limit | Sell at the limit or higher | May fill partly or not at all |
| Stop | Activate a market order when triggered | A gap can produce a worse fill than the stop |
| Stop-limit | Activate a limit order when triggered | The limit can prevent an exit |

For a buy limit of $50 with the best ask at $50.10, the instruction does not permit a $50.10 fill. If the market falls to $50, a fill still depends on available quantity and priority. Trigger conventions differ by venue and broker.

## Connect to later courses

The paper-trading lab demonstrates some order mechanics using hypothetical accounts. Strategy backtests use next-open fills and configurable costs. Neither a candle touching a price nor a stop instruction guarantees a fill at that price.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-14). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Returns, compounding, and trading costs
modules.subtitle: Measure what you keep, over the time you hold
modules.objective: Calculate profit after fees, total return with dividends, and compounded returns; distinguish realized from unrealized gains.
modules.content:
## The idea

Profit in money and return in percent answer different questions. Include the purchase cost, sale proceeds, distributions, and fees. An unrealized gain is a change in the marked value of an open position. A realized gain results from closing it. Both affect your economic wealth, and an unrealized gain can disappear before a sale.

## A worked example

Buy 10 shares at $100 and pay a $2 entry fee: the cash outlay is $1,002. Receive $10 of dividends in total. Sell all 10 shares at $110 and pay a $2 exit fee: sale proceeds are $1,098. The net gain is $1,098 + $10 − $1,002 = $106. The return on the initial cash outlay is $106 / $1,002, approximately 10.58%, before taxes.

$$R_{\text{net}}=\frac{\text{net sale proceeds}+\text{distributions}-\text{initial outlay}}{\text{initial outlay}}$$

Zero commission does not mean zero trading cost. Spreads, slippage, fund expenses, financing, and applicable taxes can affect the outcome. Avoid double counting a spread already embedded in the actual fill prices.

## Returns multiply through time

A $100 position gains 10%, reaching $110, then loses 10%, reaching $99. The combined return is −1%, although the arithmetic average of the two period returns is zero.

$$R_{\text{combined}}=(1+r_1)(1+r_2)-1$$

A decline from $100 to $80 is a 20% loss. Recovering from $80 to $100 requires a 25% gain because the new denominator is smaller. A basis point is 0.01 percentage points: 10 basis points equals 0.10%, or 0.001 as a decimal multiplier. A 10 bp fee on $1,000 is $1.

## Connect to later courses

Statistical foundations develops discounting and annualization. Backtests later separate the strategy return from the benchmark and charge costs at execution. Keep the time period, units, and cash-flow assumptions visible in every comparison.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Reading a business before buying its stock
modules.subtitle: Connect financial statements, earnings, cash, and valuation
modules.objective: Identify the three main financial statements, calculate EPS and P/E, and distinguish a low price from evidence of value.
modules.content:
## The idea

The income statement describes revenues, expenses, and profit over a period. The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity at a date. The cash-flow statement explains movements in cash from operating, investing, and financing activities. Profit and cash flow differ because recognition and payment need not happen together.

A sale on credit can increase revenue and receivables before cash arrives. Borrowing increases cash and debt without creating sales profit. Buying equipment uses cash immediately, while its accounting expense can be spread over years. Ask what caused each change before declaring the business stronger.

## A worked example

Fictional Cedar Tools reports $12 million revenue, $2 million net income available to common shareholders, and 1 million weighted-average diluted shares. Earnings per share (EPS) is $2. At a $30 share price, the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) is 15. Its balance sheet shows $15 million assets and $9 million liabilities, leaving $6 million book equity.

$$\mathrm{EPS}=\frac{\text{net income available to common}}{\text{weighted-average diluted shares}},\qquad P/E=\frac{P}{\mathrm{EPS}}$$

Suppose operating cash flow is only $0.4 million because customers have not yet paid. That does not prove fraud, but it raises a useful question about collections and working capital. A second company with a P/E of 8 may be cheaper relative to reported earnings, or those earnings may be about to decline. The multiple alone cannot decide.

## Price, value, and available evidence

Price is a current quote. Value is an estimate based on future cash flows, assets, and risk. Book equity is an accounting residual, not a guaranteed sale value. Compare several periods, examine debt and one-time items, and read the company's published reports.

When simulating a past decision, use only information available at that time. A December reporting period does not make a report released in March available in December. Treat a promotional post as a lead to verify, not as a financial statement.

## Connect to later courses

These distinctions prepare you for normalized earnings, net-current-asset value, senior claims, and margin of safety in Track 01.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks/evaluating-stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Risk, diversification, and position sizing
modules.subtitle: Understand what can go wrong before choosing a quantity
modules.objective: Distinguish company and market risk; calculate a hypothetical position size and explain why stops do not cap every loss.
modules.content:
## The idea

Company risk comes from a particular issuer, such as a failed product. Market risk can affect many investments together, such as a broad repricing of discount rates. Diversification spreads exposure, but correlated holdings can decline at the same time. Ten companies in one narrow industry may share much of the same risk.

Volatility describes variability in returns. Drawdown measures the decline from a previous portfolio peak. Neither alone captures every risk: an illiquid asset can have infrequent price changes and still be hard to sell. Consider liquidity, debt, concentration, and the ability to tolerate losses.

## A worked example

In a paper account with $10,000, a hypothetical plan allocates $100 to the loss between a $50 entry and a $48 exit trigger. Planned risk per share is $2. Dividing $100 by $2 gives 50 shares, a $2,500 position. The $100 budget is 1% of this example account; it is an illustration, not a universal sizing recommendation.

$$q=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{planned risk budget}}{\text{entry price}-\text{planned exit price}}\right\rfloor$$

If a gap leads to an actual $45 exit, the loss is $250 before costs, not $100. Fees and slippage also change the result. The calculation describes a planned scenario, not a maximum loss guarantee. Check the cash required as well as the planned risk; a cash account must be able to fund the purchase.

## Borrowing and short selling

Margin uses borrowed money to increase exposure. If $1,000 of your money and $1,000 of borrowing buy $2,000 of stock, a 10% stock loss removes $200, or 20% of your initial equity, before financing costs. The debt still needs to be repaid. Short selling sells borrowed shares and requires buying them back; rising prices can create losses beyond the initial proceeds. Detailed rules vary by account and market.

## Connect to later courses

Portfolio construction measures co-movement. Risk management studies drawdowns and tail losses. Bot engineering turns exposure limits and stale-price checks into explicit controls.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Build your first research and trading plan
modules.subtitle: Bring the fundamentals together and prepare for the advanced tracks
modules.objective: Write a testable paper-trading plan with an entry reason, order, sizing assumptions, exit conditions, costs, and review process.
modules.content:
## The idea

A plan makes a decision reviewable. Write it before observing the outcome. Specify the asset and source, the reason to enter, the evidence that would invalidate the reason, the intended holding period, the order instruction, the quantity, and the expected costs. Record actual fills separately from your intention.

Avoid evaluating a plan only by whether the last trade made money. A disciplined decision can lose; a poorly supported decision can profit by chance. Keep the record of losing trials as well as winners. Compare a strategy against a relevant benchmark over the same period using the same cost conventions.

## A worked example

In a fictional $5,000 paper account, Ari studies Harbor Foods after a published report. The hypothesis is that collections will recover; the invalidating evidence is another deterioration in receivables and operating cash flow. Ari considers 10 shares using a $20 buy limit, reserving roughly $200 plus costs. If the ask stays above $20, the order can remain unfilled.

The plan records an illustrative $18 exit trigger, a $20 planned price loss for 10 shares, and a gap scenario: an actual $15 exit would lose $50 before costs. Ari schedules a review after the next public report. There is no guarantee that the thesis works, the order fills, or the exit matches the trigger.

## Your research note

Use **Add a note** to record your own fictional plan:

1. Asset, source, and information availability date.
2. Hypothesis, holding period, and evidence against it.
3. Entry instruction, quantity, cash required, and cost assumptions.
4. Planned exit, a worse-fill scenario, and concentration check.
5. Benchmark, review date, and the result you will record even if it fails.

Confirmation bias means favoring supporting evidence and overlooking contradictions. Chasing a recent gain without checking the thesis is another common error. Add an explicit reason to wait when the evidence or data is insufficient.

## Choose what to study next

| What you want to understand | Continue with |
| --- | --- |
| Business value and a margin of safety | [Classical value investing](/curriculum/security-analysis) |
| Returns, probability, and evidence | [Statistical foundations](/curriculum/statistical-foundations) |
| Exposures and portfolio risk | [Econometrics & factor models](/curriculum/econometrics) after statistics |
| Testing repeatable rules | [Systematic strategies](/curriculum/strategy-lab) after valuation and statistics |
| Reliable automated execution | [Autonomous stock bots](/curriculum/stock-bots) after strategy testing |
| Tokens and liquidity pools | [Web3 & cryptoeconomics](/curriculum/web3) after risk fundamentals |

Complete the practice questions and final exam to check your readiness. You may revisit any lesson or retake an exam; later tracks remain available for learners who already know the basics.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks/evaluating-stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Foundations of Graham & Dodd
modules.subtitle: Distinguish a defensible investment operation from a price prediction and calculate a conservative margin of safety.
modules.objective: Distinguish a defensible investment operation from a price prediction and calculate a conservative margin of safety.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part I. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## The analytical question

Start with the security's claim, the evidence supporting payment, and the price paid. A profitable trade can have been poorly reasoned; an adverse outcome can follow a reasonable analysis. Judge the process using information available when the decision was made. Calling an asset a bond or holding a stock for years does not by itself establish investment merit.

The course treats intrinsic value as a reasoned range supported by assets, earning power, and contractual rights. Each method answers a different question. A liquidation estimate asks what might remain after disposing of assets and settling claims. A going-concern estimate assumes the business continues. Keep those assumptions visible instead of averaging incompatible numbers.

A margin of safety expresses the discount to an estimate. Its usefulness depends on the quality of that estimate. An inflated denominator can manufacture an impressive discount. A falling quotation does not automatically increase protection if the business deteriorates faster.

$$
M=1-P/V
$$

## A worked example

Fictional Alder Manufacturing trades at $60. Your estimated values are $75 under a weak operating case, $100 in the base case, and $125 in a favorable case. The margins are 20%, 40%, and 52%, respectively. With a required 30% discount to the weak-case estimate, the maximum price is $75 × 0.70 = $52.50. The base case passes; the conservative case fails.

This rule does not assign a probability to loss. If an unrecorded obligation destroys $30 of per-share value, even the weak-case estimate was inadequate. Your memo must identify what could make the analysis wrong and what evidence would cause a revision.

## Research discipline

Write a dated decision with four lines: claim purchased, conservative value range, evidence that could impair it, and maximum acceptable price. Keep the market quotation in a separate column from the valuation inputs. Revisit business facts on new information; avoid changing the estimate merely to justify a position already held.

Use the optional worksheet to vary price and value independently. Its accompanying cash-only price simulation is a technical container; it does not test whether your estimate is correct.
modules.code:
price = 60
value = 100
print("Margin of safety:", round((1 - price / value) * 100, 1), "%")
print("Conservative maximum price:", 75 * 0.70)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: At a price of $54 and weak-case value of $72, apply a 30% required discount. Write a decision and name one fact that could reduce value.
assignment.solution: The discount is 25%; the maximum price is $50.40. The stated rule does not permit purchase at $54. A customer loss, debt maturity, or impaired asset could lower the denominator; the numerical discount alone is insufficient.

exercise.question: At a price of $60 and intrinsic value of $100, what is the margin of safety?
exercise.explanation: Subtract price divided by value from one: 1 − 60/100 = 40%.

exercises.question: At a price of $60 and intrinsic value of $100, what is the margin of safety?
exercises.explanation: Subtract price divided by value from one: 1 − 60/100 = 40%.

exercises.question: Which change weakens a margin-of-safety conclusion?
options: Using an optimistic value without testing downside
exercises.explanation: A large apparent discount can be created by an unsupported optimistic value estimate.

modules.title: Build an evidence file
modules.subtitle: Separate reported facts, analytical adjustments, and assumptions in a dated research record.
modules.objective: Separate reported facts, analytical adjustments, and assumptions in a dated research record.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part I. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## From information to evidence

A security analysis is an argument supported by traceable information. Build a file that another analyst can reconstruct: document date, period covered, currency, units, scope of consolidation, and the exact item used. Published accounts, governing security documents, and management explanations answer different questions. Agreement among several data vendors may simply reflect one shared source.

Use three columns: **reported**, **adjusted**, and **assumed**. The first preserves the original observation. The second documents an explicit reconciliation. The third records a judgment with a reason and sensitivity range. Never silently replace a reported loss with a favorable estimate.

Contemporary filings are a course application of evidence discipline, not a claim about 1940 reporting rules. The [SEC financial-statement guide](https://www.sec.gov/investor/pubs/begfinstmtguide.htm) provides a starting reference for the different statements and their notes. Use the issuer's actual reporting policy when doing a real analysis.

$$
\text{Receivables intensity}=AR/\text{sales}
$$

## A worked example

Alder's year-end accounts report revenue of $240 million and receivables of $48 million. The previous year shows $200 million and $30 million. Revenue rose 20%; receivables rose 60%. Year-end receivables divided by annual sales rose from 15% to 20%. That is an investigation signal, not proof of fabrication: acquisitions, seasonality, customer terms, or collection trouble could explain it.

The filing was released on March 15. A January 31 historical decision cannot use its contents merely because the accounting period ended in December. Record both period-end and availability dates. Restated figures need their own publication date.

## A reproducible research packet

Preserve the original units and reconcile any restatement before comparing years. Record unanswered questions rather than filling gaps with plausible-looking numbers. A strong packet includes a statement bridge, a claims schedule, a list of key estimates, and an opposing interpretation of the same evidence. A weak packet contains ratios without definitions.

A discrepancy is a reason to investigate. Decide what additional document would discriminate between a benign explanation and an impaired business before changing your value estimate.
modules.code:
print("Revenue growth (%):", (240 / 200 - 1) * 100)
print("Receivables growth (%):", (48 / 30 - 1) * 100)
print("Receivables / sales:", 48 / 240)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Prepare a three-column evidence log for sales of 300, receivables of 90, and a management assertion that collections are normal. The prior receivables/sales ratio was 20%.
assignment.solution: Reported: 300 sales and 90 receivables, with dates and units. Calculated: 30% intensity, up 10 percentage points. Assumed: no collection impairment, if used at all. Request aging and subsequent receipts; management's assertion does not independently establish recoverability.

exercise.explanation: 50 / 250 = 20%; this simplified ratio uses year-end receivables, not an average balance.

modules.title: Value ranges and the limits of precision
modules.subtitle: Reconcile asset and earnings evidence without double counting or disguising uncertainty.
modules.objective: Reconcile asset and earnings evidence without double counting or disguising uncertainty.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part I. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Choose a valuation premise

An estimate has meaning only under a stated premise. An operating factory may be worth more as part of a profitable business than as equipment sold separately. A loss-making business may consume its cash before owners realize an asset surplus. A single spreadsheet total can hide these mutually exclusive paths.

Distinguish a screening value, a full analytical estimate, and a transaction price. A screen narrows the research universe. A full estimate examines business economics and claims. A transaction price also reflects bargaining, control, financing, and timing. None is automatically interchangeable with the others.

Precision should follow evidence. Use a range wide enough to reflect uncertain margins, required returns, recoveries, and timing. Do not assign probabilities merely to make a weighted average look scientific. If you do use probabilities, explain where they came from and test alternative weights.

$$
V_{equity}=V_{operations}+\text{excess cash}-\text{senior claims}
$$

## A worked example

Alder's continuing operations are estimated at $180–220 million. Excess cash is $20 million; debt is $60 million; diluted shares are 10 million. Equity value is $140–180 million, or $14–18 per share. Separately, a liquidation worksheet produces $9 per share after all claims and closure costs.

Do not add the $9 liquidation value to the $14–18 operating range. The factory and receivables supporting operations are already inside the enterprise estimate. Only genuinely nonoperating assets excluded from that estimate can be added separately. Nor does $9 establish an assured floor if liquidation is neither feasible nor timely.

## Make uncertainty decision-relevant

At a $13 quote, the discount to $14 is only about 7.1%; the discount to $18 is about 27.8%. Selecting the upper endpoint changes the answer without changing the business. State which endpoint governs your decision and why.

The useful output is a decision boundary: what must be true for the proposed price to be justified? Then seek evidence about those assumptions. An unresolved liability or uncertain ownership right may justify withholding a conclusion even when the arithmetic is easy.

assignment.prompt: Value operations at 150–190, add 15 of excess cash, deduct 45 of debt, and use 8 million shares. Explain whether you may also add the operating inventory's liquidation proceeds.
assignment.solution: Equity is 120–160, or $15–20 per share. Operating inventory is already part of the going concern; adding its liquidation proceeds would double count the same economic resources.

exercise.question: Operations worth 100, excess cash 10, debt 30, and 5 shares give what equity value per share?
exercise.explanation: (100 + 10 − 30) / 5 = $16 per share, using consistent company-wide units.

exercises.question: Operations worth 100, excess cash 10, debt 30, and 5 shares give what equity value per share?
exercises.explanation: (100 + 10 − 30) / 5 = $16 per share, using consistent company-wide units.

exercises.question: When can a separate asset be added to an operating valuation?
options: When it is excluded from the operating estimate and available to owners after claims
exercises.explanation: The asset must represent an additional claim on value rather than an input already supporting operating earnings.

modules.title: Bond safety and earnings coverage
modules.subtitle: Evaluate a fixed claim using weak-period coverage, liquidity, and the issuer's business resilience.
modules.objective: Evaluate a fixed claim using weak-period coverage, liquidity, and the issuer's business resilience.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part II. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Begin with the obligation

A bond promises specified payments, but the issuer must generate or obtain the resources to make them. The contract limits the holder's upside while a serious impairment can impose a large loss. Investigate the reasons a payment could fail before comparing attractive yields.

Coverage measures a flow of earnings against a flow of charges. State whether your numerator is before interest, taxes, depreciation, or rent. A ratio that removes economically necessary costs may overstate protection. Use several years and a deliberately weak operating case. Historical survival is evidence, not a guarantee that tomorrow's industry structure will resemble yesterday's.

A high coverage ratio cannot settle a near-term maturity if cash is inaccessible and refinancing is unavailable. Add a maturity schedule and a source-of-payment analysis. Cash at a subsidiary may not be freely distributable to the entity that issued the bond.

$$
\text{Interest coverage}=EBIT/\text{interest}
$$

## A worked example

Alder earns $120 million before interest and tax and owes $30 million of annual interest. Coverage is 4.0 times. In a weak year EBIT falls to $45 million, leaving 1.5 times coverage. If necessary recurring costs were excluded from EBIT, restore them before relying on either ratio.

Suppose $100 million of principal also matures next year, while accessible cash is $20 million and expected cash remaining after operations and interest is $25 million. The $55 million funding gap remains even though annual interest is covered. Refinancing is a possible source, not cash already on hand.

## An exclusion worksheet

Record business cyclicality, weak-period coverage, cash accessibility, maturity concentration, collateral quality, and restrictions on new claims. An unusually high yield should prompt a search for the corresponding risk. Do not let the quoted return repair a weak payment case.

No single coverage threshold works across all issuers. Define a policy for the case and explain its economic basis. A cyclical producer and a regulated utility can have different sources of uncertainty even with identical current ratios.
modules.code:
for ebit in [120, 45]:
    print("Interest coverage:", ebit / 30)
print("Maturity funding gap:", 100 - 20 - 25)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Stress EBIT from 90 to 36 with annual interest of 18. Separately assess a maturity of 80 against cash of 15 and internally generated cash of 20.
assignment.solution: Coverage falls from 5.0 to 2.0 times. The maturity gap is 45. Adequate interest coverage alone does not provide the principal payment; document a credible source or classify refinancing as unresolved.

exercise.question: EBIT is 90 and interest expense is 30. What is coverage?

exercises.question: EBIT is 90 and interest expense is 30. What is coverage?

modules.title: Seniority, collateral, and recovery
modules.subtitle: Build a simplified claim waterfall and distinguish collateral value from the issuer's total asset value.
modules.objective: Build a simplified claim waterfall and distinguish collateral value from the issuer's total asset value.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part II. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Identify who owes whom

Read the exact issuer and the claim's rank. A mortgage on one asset does not create a claim on every asset in a corporate group. A parent-company creditor can depend on residual distributions from subsidiaries whose own creditors must first be satisfied. Guarantees can change that picture; their scope matters.

Collateral protection depends on realizable proceeds after costs and competing claims. Book value is a historical accounting measure, while recovery depends on sale conditions, asset specificity, and enforceable rights. A pledge over obsolete equipment can offer little practical protection despite a large recorded balance.

The following waterfall is an arithmetic teaching model with stipulated priority and no dispute. Real legal priority, insolvency expenses, guarantees, and intercreditor terms require the actual documents; this lesson does not supply a jurisdictional rule.

$$
R_{junior}=\min(D_j,\max(0,A-D_s))/D_j
$$

## A worked example

A ring-fenced collateral pool realizes $70 million net of stipulated sale costs. The first-ranking secured claim is $50 million; a junior claim is $30 million. The senior holder recovers $50 million in full. Only $20 million remains, so the junior recovery is 20 / 30 = 66.7%. Equity receives nothing from this pool.

If proceeds fall to $40 million, the senior recovery becomes 80%, and junior recovery is zero. Label these outcomes as scenario recoveries. They are not default probabilities or present values. Waiting two years for a recovery also changes its economic value.

## Draw the claims map

List assets by owner, security interests by claimant, and residual transfers between entities. State whether each liability is recourse to the pool, another entity, or both. Avoid assigning the same collateral proceeds in full to two different creditors.

A recovery estimate should include a timing range and a sensitivity to realizable proceeds. Investigate whether maintaining the asset until sale consumes cash. Coverage and collateral complement one another: one studies payment from ongoing activity, the other protection if that activity fails.
modules.code:
for assets in [70, 40]:
    senior = min(50, assets)
    junior = min(30, max(0, assets - senior))
    print("Senior and junior recovery:", senior / 50, junior / 30)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: At 95, senior receives 60, junior 35 (70%), equity zero. At 55, senior receives 55 (91.67%), junior and equity zero. These results depend on the stipulated priority and net proceeds.

exercise.explanation: After 60 is paid, 15 remains for the junior claim of 30, giving 50%.

modules.title: Covenants and the deterioration of protection
modules.subtitle: Read a covenant as a defined test and model how additional borrowing changes creditor protection.
modules.objective: Read a covenant as a defined test and model how additional borrowing changes creditor protection.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part II. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Protection can change after purchase

An issuer can weaken an initially sound bond by adding debt, transferring assets, or distributing cash. Contractual restrictions can limit those actions, but the precise definitions and exceptions matter. An earnings test based on an adjusted metric can behave differently from the ordinary income statement.

For any stipulated covenant, record numerator, denominator, measurement date, threshold, permitted adjustments, and what happens if the test is failed. Do not infer the remedy from the word covenant alone. This exercise uses invented contract terms, not a claim about standard legal protections.

A limit on new borrowing is different from a test that must be satisfied continuously or periodically. Passing an incurrence test today does not ensure adequate payment resources in a later downturn. Likewise, covenant headroom is not identical to economic safety.

$$
\text{Incremental interest capacity}=EBIT/c-I_0
$$

## A worked example

An invented bond permits additional debt only if EBIT divided by total annual interest remains at least 3.0 times immediately after the new issue. Current EBIT is $90 million and interest is $20 million. The maximum permitted annual interest is $30 million, so contractual incremental interest capacity is $10 million under these definitions.

Management proposes debt adding $8 million of interest. Pro-forma coverage is 90 / 28 = 3.21 times, so this test passes. At stressed EBIT of $56 million, coverage would be only 2.0 times. The contract's initial permission has not removed operating risk.

## Analyze the incentives

Ask who benefits from a dividend, acquisition, or refinancing and which security bears the added downside. Compare cash transferred to owners with the remaining coverage cushion. Read definitions before importing a ratio from a data service.

Your report should show the contract calculation beside an economic calculation using recurring costs. Differences can be informative without implying that either definition is mathematically wrong. The decision is whether the remaining protection is adequate at the proposed price.

ebit = 90
threshold = 3
interest = 20
print("Additional interest capacity:", ebit / threshold - interest)
print("Pro-forma coverage:", ebit / (interest + 8))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: A stipulated test requires 4-times coverage. EBIT is 120 and existing interest is 24. Can an issue adding 8 of interest pass? Explain economic versus contractual protection.
assignment.solution: Maximum interest is 30, leaving capacity of 6. Proposed total interest of 32 gives 3.75 times, so the issue fails this test. Even a passing issue would require a separate stress and liquidity analysis.

exercise.question: EBIT of 80 and a required coverage of 4 allow total interest of:
exercise.explanation: 80 / 4 = 20 is total permitted interest under the stipulated definition.

exercises.question: EBIT of 80 and a required coverage of 4 allow total interest of:
exercises.explanation: 80 / 4 = 20 is total permitted interest under the stipulated definition.

exercises.question: Why read the covenant's earnings definition?
options: Adjustments can materially change the measured headroom
exercises.explanation: Permitted add-backs and deductions can change coverage even when the operating business is unchanged.

modules.title: Price, yield, calls, and reinvestment
modules.subtitle: Separate coupon income from contractual return and identify how call rights limit upside.
modules.objective: Separate coupon income from contractual return and identify how call rights limit upside.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part II. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## A quoted yield needs a cash-flow schedule

Coupon rate divides the annual coupon by face value. Current yield divides it by market price. Yield to maturity is the discount rate equating price with promised coupons and principal, assuming those payments occur. These quantities answer different questions. A discount to par contributes to promised maturity return; a premium can be lost as the bond approaches repayment.

Before solving a yield, write every payment date and amount. For a callable security, also model the issuer's right to redeem early. When rates fall, an attractive coupon may be removed just when reinvestment opportunities become less attractive. The holder does not control the most favorable repayment scenario.

A promised yield does not adjust itself for default risk or transaction costs. Comparing two securities solely by yield can conceal differences in payment reliability, maturity, embedded options, and liquidity.

$$
R_{1y}=(C+F-P)/P
$$

## A worked example

An invented one-year bond has $100 face value and a $6 final coupon. At a price of $98, its promised one-year return is (106 − 98) / 98 = 8.16%. Current yield is 6 / 98 = 6.12%. The difference comes from receiving $100 principal after paying $98.

Now consider a different bond purchased at $105 that the issuer may call in one year at $100, with one $6 coupon before redemption. Under that stipulated call scenario, proceeds are $106 and the return is only 0.95%. Looking only at its 5.71% current yield misses the $5 capital loss.

## Compare complete alternatives

Build a table of price, payment dates, maturity proceeds, possible call proceeds, and key protection. Use consistent compounding and include accrued interest where the actual transaction requires it. A higher coupon can be worth less if call terms sharply constrain favorable outcomes.

A useful analyst explains both how the quoted return is calculated and what events prevent it from being earned. Credit analysis and valuation belong in the same decision.
modules.code:
print("One-year maturity return (%):", round((106 - 98) / 98 * 100, 2))
print("One-year call return (%):", round((106 - 105) / 105 * 100, 2))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.

assignment.prompt: Pay 103 for a bond with one coupon of 4 before a stipulated one-year call at 100. Compare call return with current yield.
assignment.solution: Call return is (104 − 103) / 103 = 0.97%. Current yield is 4 / 103 = 3.88%. The premium loss explains the difference; neither calculation guarantees the issuer's payment.

modules.subtitle: Analyze dividend priority, arrears, and the difference between preferred equity and debt.

modules.content:
## Read the preference

Preferred shares combine a stated priority with issuer-specific terms. A fixed dividend rate can resemble a coupon economically, but preferred stock is equity and its payment rights are defined by its terms. Do not assume that a missed dividend creates the same remedies as missed bond interest.

Check whether dividends are cumulative, whether arrears restrict common distributions, whether the issue participates beyond its stated dividend, and whether the issuer can redeem it. Voting rights or other protections may change after specified events. Analyze the actual instrument; the label preferred is insufficient.

For a cumulative issue, unpaid dividends can accumulate as a priority before common dividends under the stipulated terms. Accumulation does not place cash in the holder's account. A profitable recovery may still leave a long wait before common shareholders receive distributions.

$$
D_{pref}=\text{preference}\times\text{dividend rate}
$$

## A worked example

An invented cumulative preferred issue has $20 million of liquidation preference and a 6% annual dividend. Its annual requirement is $1.2 million. Two omitted annual dividends create $2.4 million of arrears. Under the case terms, common dividends cannot resume until arrears and the current preferred dividend are satisfied.

If $5 million is lawfully available for distributions this year, paying $2.4 million of arrears plus $1.2 million current preference leaves $1.4 million for common holders. If only $2 million is available, it cannot satisfy all preferred requirements. The accumulated claim should not be confused with evidence of payment capacity.

## Evaluate the junior creditor-like position

Study earnings after interest and tax because preferred dividends are paid from resources remaining after senior obligations. Compare the preference with common equity support and inspect whether assets can be transferred away. A low market price can indicate an impaired claim rather than an exceptional income opportunity.

Write a distribution waterfall separate from a liquidation waterfall. The rights and amounts applicable to one need not be identical to those in the other. Treat the simplified arithmetic as the beginning of document analysis.

annual = 20 * 0.06
arrears = annual * 2
print("Annual preference:", annual)
print("Residual distribution:", 5 - arrears - annual)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: A cumulative issue has preference of 30, an 8% dividend, and three years of arrears. Under terms requiring arrears plus the current dividend first, allocate an available distribution of 12.
assignment.solution: Annual dividend is 2.4; arrears are 7.2. Total priority is 9.6, leaving 2.4 for common holders if the distribution is permitted. This says nothing about the separate liquidation recovery.

exercise.question: A preference of 50 with a 4% dividend requires annually:
exercise.explanation: 50 × 4% = 2 in the same monetary units as the preference.

exercises.question: A preference of 50 with a 4% dividend requires annually:
exercises.explanation: 50 × 4% = 2 in the same monetary units as the preference.

exercises.question: Cumulative arrears establish:
options: A claim priority under the issue's terms, not assured payment
exercises.explanation: Arrears describe a contractual preference; the issuer still needs resources and the applicable conditions to pay.

modules.title: Convertible securities and participation
modules.subtitle: Calculate conversion value and premium while testing the quality of the underlying fixed claim.
modules.objective: Calculate conversion value and premium while testing the quality of the underlying fixed claim.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part III. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Two sources of value, two sources of error

A convertible security offers a fixed or preferred claim together with a right to exchange it for common shares on stated terms. The conversion feature can provide participation in favorable business outcomes. That attraction does not repair an unsound issuer: the bond's protection and the stock's value may deteriorate together.

Identify face value, conversion ratio, adjustment provisions, maturity, and redemption terms. The conversion price is face value divided by shares delivered. Conversion value is the current share price multiplied by that ratio. A quoted convertible can trade above immediate conversion value because its remaining rights have value, but the size of the premium matters.

A so-called bond floor is an estimate of the comparable nonconvertible claim, not an assured market minimum. Its assumptions include credit quality, rates, and liquidity. A falling share price caused by business distress can coincide with a falling fixed-claim value.

$$
V_{conversion}=nP_s;\quad \text{premium}=P_c/V_{conversion}-1
$$

## A worked example

An invented $1,000 bond converts into 25 common shares. Its conversion price is $40. At a common share price of $36, conversion value is $900. If the convertible costs $1,080, its premium over conversion value is $180, or 20% of $900.

Suppose a comparable straight claim is estimated at $850. Paying $1,080 includes $230 above that estimate for the package's additional features and differences. Do not add $850 and $900: the holder normally chooses between claims rather than receiving both principal and the full conversion shares.

## Investigate dilution and forced decisions

Model the share count if every relevant security converts. Compare conversion benefits with coupons or dividends surrendered. An issuer call may force a decision sooner than an investor expected. Read the timing and adjustment provisions before describing the instrument as a bond with free upside.

Your memo should show both a weak credit case and a favorable conversion case. The most attractive feature can dominate attention while the protection needed in adversity remains unexamined.

ratio = 25
conversion = ratio * 36
print("Conversion price:", 1000 / ratio)
print("Conversion value:", conversion)
print("Premium (%):", round((1080 / conversion - 1) * 100, 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: A 1,000-face convertible exchanges for 20 shares. The stock is 45 and the convertible is 990. Calculate conversion price, conversion value, and premium; explain why principal and conversion value cannot simply be added.
assignment.solution: Conversion price is 50, conversion value 900, and premium 10%. Conversion exchanges the fixed claim for shares under the stipulated terms; adding both assumes receipt of mutually exclusive payoffs.

exercise.question: A 1,000-face bond converts into 40 shares. Its conversion price is:
exercise.explanation: Divide face value by conversion shares: 1,000 / 40 = $25.

exercises.question: A 1,000-face bond converts into 40 shares. Its conversion price is:
exercises.explanation: Divide face value by conversion shares: 1,000 / 40 = $25.

exercises.question: Why can an estimated straight-bond floor fall with the stock?
options: Credit quality may deteriorate at the same time
It is legally fixed at par
exercises.explanation: Business distress can reduce both debt recovery prospects and equity value; the floor is an estimate.

modules.title: Common ownership and dividend policy
modules.subtitle: Evaluate distributions and retention through the economic interests of common shareholders.
modules.objective: Evaluate distributions and retention through the economic interests of common shareholders.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part IV. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Earnings belong to a business before they become cash to owners

Common shareholders hold the residual interest. They benefit when retained resources earn worthwhile returns or when surplus resources are distributed sensibly. Reported profit is neither automatically distributable cash nor proof that retention benefits owners.

Study the reason for retention: working capital, maintenance, expansion, debt reduction, or an acquisition. Distinguish necessary reinvestment from discretionary growth. A business that must reinvest heavily just to maintain earnings may have less distributable capacity than an equally profitable business with modest maintenance needs.

Dividend yield describes one component of return. A high payout can be financed by borrowing or asset sales and may be unsustainable. A low payout can reflect attractive opportunities or poor capital discipline. Evaluate the use of retained funds rather than assuming either policy is superior.

$$
\text{Payout}=D/E;\quad \text{retention}=1-D/E
$$

## A worked example

Alder earns $30 million for common shareholders, pays $12 million of dividends, and retains $18 million. Its payout ratio is 40%; retention is 60%. Suppose management proposes a project costing the retained $18 million that is expected to add $1.8 million of sustainable annual profit. The implied incremental return is 10% under the case assumptions.

If the project instead adds only $0.9 million, the incremental return is 5%. The accounting act of retaining money is identical, but the economic opportunity differs. Compare the uncertain return with an appropriately chosen requirement and examine whether the estimate includes all additional costs.

## Observe results over time

Track incremental capital committed and subsequent operating performance. Acquisitions, share issuance, and changes in business mix complicate attribution. Do not compare a single year's total profit with a single year's retention and call that the return on new capital.

Write an owner-focused question: what can the company do with the next dollar that I could not accomplish as well outside it? Answer with evidence about business opportunities, management decisions, and claims on the cash.

earnings = 30
dividends = 12
print("Payout:", dividends / earnings)
print("Incremental project return:", 1.8 / (earnings - dividends))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Earnings are 40, dividends 10, and a project uses all retained earnings to add 2.4 of recurring annual profit. Calculate payout, retention, and incremental return. Identify an assumption to investigate.
assignment.solution: Payout is 25%, retention 75%, and project return 2.4 / 30 = 8%. Investigate whether the additional profit is sustainable and net of maintenance, working-capital, and financing effects relevant to the chosen comparison.

exercise.question: Earnings of 25 and dividends of 10 give a payout ratio of:
exercise.explanation: 10 / 25 = 40%; the remaining 60% is retained in this simplified case.

exercises.question: Earnings of 25 and dividends of 10 give a payout ratio of:
exercises.explanation: 10 / 25 = 40%; the remaining 60% is retained in this simplified case.

exercises.question: What best supports a retention policy?
options: Management's preference for a larger company
Evidence that incremental investment creates sufficient value for its risk
exercises.explanation: Retention should be judged by the prospective and realized economics of the resources kept in the business.

modules.title: Share count, repurchases, and owner outcomes
modules.subtitle: Distinguish mechanical EPS changes from an improvement in the value owned by continuing shareholders.
modules.objective: Distinguish mechanical EPS changes from an improvement in the value owned by continuing shareholders.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part IV. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Keep the denominator honest

A per-share measure combines company-wide resources with a claim count. Changes in either can alter the result. Stock splits change units; issuance changes the ownership fraction; repurchases use company resources to retire claims. Dilution analysis must include the relevant contingent securities under clearly stated assumptions.

An increase in earnings per share after a repurchase does not establish value creation. The company has spent cash or taken on debt. What matters is the value surrendered compared with the value of claims retired, including financing effects and remaining resilience.

Use a consistent date and share basis. A period's reported EPS may use a weighted-average denominator, while an estimate of value today uses the claims outstanding or expected to participate today. Explain the difference instead of mixing the two measures.

$$
V_{after/share}=(V_{before}-C)/(N-C/P_{buyback})
$$

## A worked example

Alder has equity value of $100 million, including $20 million of genuinely excess cash, and 10 million shares. Estimated value is $10 per share. It spends $20 million repurchasing 2.5 million shares at $8. Remaining equity value is $80 million and remaining shares are 7.5 million, giving $10.67 per share under the unchanged operating-value assumption.

If it instead spends the same $20 million at $12, it retires about 1.667 million shares. Remaining value per share is $80 / 8.333 = $9.60. The repurchase label is the same; the purchase price changes the owner outcome.

## Check the financing and opportunity cost

The example assumes the cash was not required to operate, no taxes or transaction costs, and no change in business value. Borrowing for a repurchase can alter risk and required returns. Buying shares before a severe operating deterioration can weaken liquidity.

Compare the repurchase with debt reduction, distributions, and productive investment. A careful memo reconciles cash used, shares retired, new obligations, and the value of each continuing claim.

assignment.prompt: Equity value is 240 with 20 shares. Spend 24 of excess cash buying shares at 8. Compute remaining per-share value and contrast a two-for-one split.
assignment.solution: Three shares are retired, leaving value of 216 and 17 shares: $12.71 versus $12 initially. A two-for-one split alone halves value per share and doubles shares, leaving each owner's economic interest unchanged.

exercise.question: A two-for-one split, with no other change, does what to ownership percentage?
exercise.explanation: Both the owner's shares and total shares double, so the fraction owned is unchanged.

exercises.question: A two-for-one split, with no other change, does what to ownership percentage?
exercises.explanation: Both the owner's shares and total shares double, so the fraction owned is unchanged.

exercises.question: Why is higher EPS after a repurchase insufficient evidence of value creation?
options: The cash spent and price paid also affect continuing owners
exercises.explanation: EPS can rise mechanically while the company overpays for shares or weakens its financing position.

modules.title: Normalize earning power
modules.subtitle: Reconcile reported earnings to a defensible range of recurring profit across a business cycle.
modules.objective: Reconcile reported earnings to a defensible range of recurring profit across a business cycle.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part V. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Decide what can recur

Earning power is an estimate of what a business can sustain under stated conditions. Start from reported results and construct an explicit bridge. Remove a disposal gain if it does not represent ongoing operations. Restore an omitted recurring cost. Treat a charge called exceptional skeptically if similar charges appear repeatedly.

Use a history long enough to observe relevant business conditions, but recognize structural changes. A simple average of a business that has doubled capacity or lost its main product can be misleading. Adjust for changes in scale and economics before treating the past as representative.

Normalize both favorable and unfavorable items. Adding back every loss while keeping every gain biases the result. Maintain consistent tax treatment and share counts. Present a range if judgments about recurrence cannot be resolved confidently.

$$
E_{normalized}=E_{reported}-\text{nonrecurring gains}+\text{justified adjustments}
$$

## A worked example

Alder's recurring EPS over five comparable years is $2, $3, $4, $3, and $3. The arithmetic average is $3. A separate after-tax property disposal adds $2 to the final year's reported EPS, taking it to $5. Using $5 as sustainable profit would capitalize a gain that cannot repeat without another asset sale.

Suppose the final year also includes a $0.40 after-tax plant closure charge. If this truly concludes a unique exit, an analyst might exclude it when estimating future earnings. If closures occur as part of an ongoing restructuring program, some recurring allowance may be necessary. The label alone cannot decide the adjustment.

## Build the bridge before the multiple

Record reported EPS, each after-tax adjustment, the supporting evidence, and adjusted EPS. Then compare margins, utilization, customer concentration, and required reinvestment across years. A multiple applied to a weakly supported earnings number cannot rescue the analysis.

A conservative conclusion might use $2.50–3.00 until demand and cost stability are better established. Report why the lower endpoint differs from the historical mean. The exercise is economic judgment disciplined by reconciliation, not a search for the largest allowable add-back.
modules.code:
eps = [2, 3, 4, 3, 3]
print("Average recurring EPS:", sum(eps) / len(eps))
print("Reported EPS including disposal:", eps[-1] + 2)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Reported EPS is 6, including a 2 after-tax disposal gain and a 0.5 after-tax charge. Prepare normalized EPS assuming the charge is either recurring or genuinely isolated.
assignment.solution: Keeping the recurring charge gives 6 − 2 = 4. Excluding a genuinely isolated charge gives 4.5. Document evidence for the choice; do not use the higher result just because it supports the desired price.

exercise.question: Which item most clearly calls for a normalization adjustment?
options: A gain from selling the headquarters
exercise.explanation: A disposal gain generally does not describe recurring operating earning power.

exercises.question: Which item most clearly calls for a normalization adjustment?
options: A gain from selling the headquarters
exercises.explanation: A disposal gain generally does not describe recurring operating earning power.

exercises.question: A company reports restructuring charges every year. The best starting treatment is:
options: Add all of them back automatically
Investigate whether a recurring economic cost remains
exercises.explanation: Repeated charges may reflect continuing costs; recurrence must be assessed before excluding them.

modules.title: Depreciation and the cost of staying in business
modules.subtitle: Explain how asset lives affect reported profit and distinguish noncash expense from avoidable economic cost.
modules.objective: Explain how asset lives affect reported profit and distinguish noncash expense from avoidable economic cost.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part V. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## An accounting allocation represents a real resource

Depreciation spreads an asset's recorded cost across accounting periods. The charge is noncash in the current period, but the equipment was paid for and may eventually need replacement. Adding depreciation back to earnings without allowing for necessary reinvestment can exaggerate resources available to owners.

Compare useful-life assumptions with wear, technology, utilization, and replacement plans. An extension of estimated life reduces annual expense immediately even if no additional cash is generated. Conversely, accounting depreciation may exceed or fall short of current maintenance spending for legitimate reasons.

Separate maintenance from growth expenditure where evidence permits. The distinction is an analytical estimate, not a license to classify every costly project as optional expansion. A capacity project can include replacement of worn-out equipment; sustaining a competitive position can require investment beyond physical repair.

$$
D=(\text{cost}-\text{residual})/\text{life}
$$

## A worked example

A machine costs $60 million with no assumed residual value. Straight-line depreciation over ten years is $6 million annually. Extending the assumed life to fifteen years reduces annual expense to $4 million, raising pretax profit by $2 million without changing current receipts or payments.

Alder reports EBITDA of $30 million. Estimated recurring maintenance investment is $7 million and a representative tax charge is $5 million. A simplified pre-financing, pre-working-capital cash proxy is $18 million. EBITDA alone would exceed that proxy by $12 million. This is not a complete cash-flow valuation: working capital, financing, and other claims remain to be considered.

## Reconcile accounting and economics

Inspect asset age, gross and net carrying amounts, accumulated depreciation, capital spending, and capacity changes. Explain differences over several periods. One year's unusually low capital spending may reflect deferred maintenance that raises future requirements.

Write a sensitivity for the maintenance estimate and show its effect on distributable resources. A business whose value depends on permanently negligible replacement spending needs particularly strong evidence.

print("Ten-year depreciation:", 60 / 10)
print("Fifteen-year depreciation:", 60 / 15)
print("Simplified cash proxy:", 30 - 7 - 5)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.

assignment.prompt: An asset costing 80 with no residual is depreciated over 8 rather than 10 years. Calculate the annual difference and explain why adding it back is not automatically justified.
assignment.solution: Annual depreciation is 10 versus 8, a difference of 2. Choosing a longer economic life requires evidence. Depreciation is noncash this year but represents capital consumption that may require future replacement.

exercise.question: An asset costing 45 with zero residual and a 9-year life has annual straight-line depreciation of:
exercise.explanation: 45 / 9 = 5 under the stipulated straight-line method.

exercises.question: An asset costing 45 with zero residual and a 9-year life has annual straight-line depreciation of:
exercises.explanation: 45 / 9 = 5 under the stipulated straight-line method.

exercises.question: Why can EBITDA overstate funds available to owners?
options: It already deducts every cash cost
Maintenance investment, taxes, and other uses can remain
exercises.explanation: EBITDA does not by itself deduct required capital spending, taxes, working capital, or financing uses.

modules.title: Inventory, reserves, and profit comparability
modules.subtitle: Trace how inventory and reserve estimates can shift profit between periods without equivalent economic improvement.
modules.objective: Trace how inventory and reserve estimates can shift profit between periods without equivalent economic improvement.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part V. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Accounting choices affect the comparison

Inventory costs become expenses when goods are sold, subject to the reporting framework and the firm's policies. In a changing cost environment, the expense assigned to current sales can differ from the cost of replacing the goods. A favorable reported margin may therefore reflect the release of older, cheaper stock rather than stronger pricing power.

Reserve estimates introduce another source of timing differences. A reduction in an allowance can raise earnings today while future collections or obligations remain uncertain. Study the reserve roll-forward: opening balance, additions, actual uses, acquisitions, and closing balance. A reserve release deserves an explanation tied to new evidence.

This lesson uses simplified economic comparisons. It does not prescribe a particular modern accounting treatment. Real policies differ across reporting frameworks and asset classes; first establish the method the issuer actually uses.

$$
GP_{replacement}=Q(P-C_{replacement})
$$

## A worked example

Alder sells 100 units for $15 each. Their recorded cost is $8 per unit, while replacing them would cost $11. Reported gross profit on this simplified batch is $700. A replacement-cost comparison gives $400. The $300 difference matters if the firm must replenish inventory to sustain sales.

Separately, an allowance falls by $2 million solely because management changes an estimate. Pretax profit rises by $2 million in the case. That increase does not represent $2 million of additional customer cash received. Whether the release is justified depends on the underlying evidence.

## Ask what repeats

Compare inventory quantities, unit costs, sales prices, write-downs, and turnover. Falling inventory can temporarily support cash flow while leaving the next period understocked. Rising inventory can reflect growth, seasonality, or unsold goods.

For each adjustment, preserve reported profit and show a separate economic comparison. Do not deduct the same inventory impairment twice through both a carrying-value haircut and an additional earnings charge in a valuation that already incorporates the loss.

units = 100
print("Recorded gross profit:", units * (15 - 8))
print("Replacement-cost comparison:", units * (15 - 11))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.

    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Sell 200 units at 12. Recorded cost is 7 and replacement cost is 9. Calculate both gross profits and explain the difference to an owner who must replenish inventory.
assignment.solution: Recorded gross profit is 1,000; replacement-cost comparison is 600. The 400 difference cannot be assumed distributable while maintaining the same inventory quantity at the new cost.

exercise.question: Selling 50 units at 20 with replacement cost of 14 gives replacement-cost gross profit of:
exercise.explanation: 50 × (20 − 14) = 300 before overhead and other expenses.

exercises.question: Selling 50 units at 20 with replacement cost of 14 gives replacement-cost gross profit of:
exercises.explanation: 50 × (20 − 14) = 300 before overhead and other expenses.

exercises.question: An allowance release raises profit. What should the analyst request?
options: A roll-forward and evidence supporting the revised estimate
exercises.explanation: The release is an estimate change that needs reconciliation to actual underlying developments.

modules.title: Profit, cash conversion, and financing strain
modules.subtitle: Reconcile a simplified earnings-to-cash bridge and identify when growth consumes liquidity.
modules.objective: Reconcile a simplified earnings-to-cash bridge and identify when growth consumes liquidity.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part V. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Profit can arrive before cash

An income statement recognizes economic activity under accounting rules; a cash-flow analysis asks when resources actually enter or leave. The difference can be normal and temporary. It can also reveal a business that continually reports profit while requiring external finance.

Separate noncash expenses from working-capital investment. A rise in receivables typically absorbs cash relative to recognized revenue. Additional inventory also ties up resources. Growth in operating payables can temporarily finance these uses, but suppliers may not extend terms indefinitely.

The bridge below is an original simplified contemporary worksheet. Its purpose is to continue the book's analytical habit of interrogating reported earnings. It omits many real adjustments and is not a substitute for a complete statement of cash flows.

$$
CFO\approx NI+D-\Delta AR-\Delta Inv+\Delta AP
$$

## A worked example

Alder reports net income of $20 million and depreciation of $6 million. Receivables rise by $8 million, inventory by $5 million, and operating payables by $3 million. With no other adjustments, operating cash flow is 20 + 6 − 8 − 5 + 3 = $16 million. After $7 million of capital spending, cash remaining before financing distributions is $9 million.

If receivables instead rise by $18 million, operating cash flow falls to $6 million and the amount after capital spending becomes −$1 million. Reported net income remains $20 million in this isolated sensitivity. The company must fund the difference through existing cash or financing.

## Follow the cash through the cycle

Determine whether receivable growth reflects timing or poor collection, whether inventory supports future demand, and whether payables are overdue. One period's weak conversion is not proof of low-quality earnings. Persistent unexplained divergence is more informative.

Compare cumulative earnings, cumulative cash generation, investment, and changes in financing over several years. Explain the source of distributions. A dividend paid using borrowed money does not validate the sustainability of earnings.

cfo = 20 + 6 - 8 - 5 + 3
print("Operating cash flow:", cfo)
print("Cash after capital spending:", cfo - 7)
