# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Net income is 15, depreciation 4, receivables increase 6, inventory increases 2, and payables increase 1. Calculate operating cash and cash after capital spending of 5.
assignment.solution: Operating cash is 15 + 4 − 6 − 2 + 1 = 12. Cash after spending is 7. This simplified result excludes financing and any other cash-flow adjustments; investigate whether working-capital uses will reverse.

exercise.question: An increase in operating receivables, holding other bridge items fixed, generally:
options: Adds to cash relative to profit
exercise.explanation: Recognized revenue has not yet been collected, so the receivables increase is deducted in the simplified bridge.

exercises.question: An increase in operating receivables, holding other bridge items fixed, generally:
options: Adds to cash relative to profit
exercises.explanation: Recognized revenue has not yet been collected, so the receivables increase is deducted in the simplified bridge.

exercises.question: Why compare cumulative cash conversion over several years?
options: To distinguish timing differences from persistent financing needs
exercises.explanation: Several periods can reveal whether temporary differences reverse or recurring cash shortfalls accumulate.

modules.title: Net current assets and liquidation haircuts
modules.subtitle: Calculate NCAV and a separate stressed realization estimate after every senior claim.
modules.objective: Calculate NCAV and a separate stressed realization estimate after every senior claim.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VI. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## The balance sheet is a starting inventory of claims

Net-current-asset value deducts all liabilities and applicable preferred claims from current assets. It is not ordinary working capital, which deducts only current liabilities. Long-term debt still stands ahead of common owners even when the analyst focuses only on cash, receivables, and inventory.

Recorded current assets need not realize their carrying amounts. Collection quality, obsolescence, restricted cash, and sale conditions affect recovery. Haircuts should be tied to evidence about specific assets. Fixed percentage assumptions are useful for sensitivity exercises, not universal recovery laws.

A discount to NCAV is a research screen. Check whether losses will consume the surplus, whether owners can access it, and whether unrecognized obligations or closure costs remain. A low quoted price does not force liquidation or guarantee realization.

$$
NCAV/share=(CA-TL-Pref)/N
$$

## A worked example

Alder has cash of $40 million, receivables of $60 million, inventory of $80 million, total liabilities of $70 million, no preferred claim, and 10 million common shares. NCAV is $110 million, or $11 per share. A two-thirds screening price would be approximately $7.33, using this stipulated rule.

Apply a 15% haircut to receivables and 40% to inventory. Adjusted resources become 40 + 51 + 48 = $139 million. After liabilities, $69 million remains, or $6.90 per share. Additional closure costs would reduce it further. The original $11 is not a conservative liquidation promise.

## Separate scenarios and deductions

Prepare a reported NCAV column, an orderly-realization case, and a more adverse case. Show every liability and preferred claim exactly once. Include a timeline and expected cash consumption if the thesis requires waiting.

A business can be cheap on a current-asset screen and still destroy owner value. The next analytical step is understanding whether the surplus can survive and eventually reach common shareholders.
modules.code:
ncav = (40 + 60 + 80 - 70) / 10
adjusted = (40 + 60 * 0.85 + 80 * 0.60 - 70) / 10
print("NCAV per share:", ncav)
print("Adjusted realization:", adjusted)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Use cash 20, receivables 40, inventory 50, total liabilities 45, preferred claims 5, and 5 shares. Calculate NCAV and an adjusted value using 80% receivable and 50% inventory recovery.
assignment.solution: NCAV is (110 − 45 − 5) / 5 = 12. Adjusted value is (20 + 32 + 25 − 45 − 5) / 5 = 5.4. Closure costs and waiting-period losses would require further deductions.

exercise.question: Why does NCAV subtract total liabilities?
options: Common equity is junior to all liabilities
exercise.explanation: All creditors rank ahead of the residual common-equity claim.

exercises.question: Why does NCAV subtract total liabilities?
options: Common equity is junior to all liabilities
exercises.explanation: All creditors rank ahead of the residual common-equity claim.

exercises.question: What distinguishes NCAV from ordinary working capital?
options: NCAV deducts total liabilities and applicable preferred claims
exercises.explanation: Working capital uses current liabilities; the common-owner NCAV screen must also recognize other senior claims.

modules.title: Hidden obligations and the realization clock
modules.subtitle: Stress an asset surplus for cash burn, closure costs, and claims omitted from a first-pass screen.
modules.objective: Stress an asset surplus for cash burn, closure costs, and claims omitted from a first-pass screen.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VI. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Time can consume the apparent bargain

An asset-based thesis requires more than a balance-sheet surplus. The business may continue losing cash while owners wait for a sale, restructuring, or change in policy. Management may invest the surplus in an unattractive project. A static calculation should therefore be accompanied by a timeline.

List restrictions on cash, commitments, guarantees, customer deposits, disputed obligations, and likely realization expenses. In contemporary accounts, some lease obligations and other items may already be recognized. Reconcile the claims schedule to recorded liabilities before adding any incremental estimate, so that you do not deduct the same obligation twice.

Distinguish a known liability, an estimated additional cost, and a downside contingency. Show the probability or scenario premise if relevant rather than presenting all possibilities as certain cash payments. The objective is a transparent range.

$$
V_0=(A-\text{burn}-\text{incremental costs})/(1+r)^T
$$

## A worked example

An initial asset screen leaves $40 million for common shareholders. The proposed realization takes two years. Expected net operating cash burn is $6 million each year, incremental closure costs are $5 million, and an additional obligation not included in the original claims schedule is estimated at $3 million. The residual before discounting is 40 − 12 − 5 − 3 = $20 million.

At a stipulated 10% annual discount rate, a single $20 million receipt at the end of year two has present value of about $16.53 million. This timing simplification differs from a detailed schedule in which individual costs occur earlier; state which model you use.

## Demand a path to realization

Identify who can initiate a sale or distribution, what approvals and financing are required, and what prevents delay. A catalyst is an event with a plausible mechanism, not just the hope that investors notice a low multiple.

Track the thesis through time. Compare actual cash burn with the estimate and update value when evidence changes. A lower share price cannot offset a vanishing asset surplus indefinitely.
modules.code:
residual = 40 - 6 * 2 - 5 - 3
print("Residual at realization:", residual)
print("Simplified present value:", round(residual / 1.10 ** 2, 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: A surplus of 30 faces three years of annual cash burn of 4 and incremental closure costs of 6. Calculate the residual and its value if all net proceeds arrive in year three at an 8% discount rate.
assignment.solution: Residual is 30 − 12 − 6 = 12. Discounted value is 12 / 1.08³ ≈ 9.53. A more detailed model would date each cash flow separately; delay and further burn can undermine the bargain.

modules.title: Book value, intangibles, and asset productivity
modules.subtitle: Explain why book value is neither a universal floor nor a complete account of business worth.
modules.objective: Explain why book value is neither a universal floor nor a complete account of business worth.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VI. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Interpret what the carrying amount measures

Book equity is the residual of recognized assets and liabilities under accounting conventions. It can reflect historical costs, estimates, acquisitions, and past losses. It is useful evidence about capital supplied and resources recorded, but it does not automatically measure sale proceeds or sustainable earning power.

Tangible assets may be specialized, obsolete, or costly to remove. Intangible assets can be economically valuable even when little appears on the balance sheet. Conversely, an acquisition premium recorded as goodwill does not itself establish value that a new buyer would pay.

Separate an asset's independent realization value from its contribution to an operating system. Customer relationships, trained staff, and distribution arrangements can support earnings without being readily saleable in isolation. The analytical premise determines how to treat them.

$$
\text{Tangible equity}=\text{assets}-\text{liabilities}-\text{goodwill}
$$

## A worked example

Alder reports assets of $200 million, including $50 million of goodwill, and liabilities of $120 million. Book equity is $80 million. A simple tangible-equity calculation removes goodwill, leaving $30 million. With 10 million shares, the two figures are $8 and $3 per share.

Neither figure settles value. If tangible assets can realize only $130 million in total after removing goodwill and considering recoveries, the residual before further costs is $10 million. Alternatively, a durable profitable business could have going-concern value exceeding book equity. Those are separate hypotheses requiring different evidence.

## Connect assets to earning power

Compare the resources required to generate normalized profit with the profit actually earned. A large asset base earning very little may signal poor economics, excess capacity, or understated future improvement. A small recorded asset base earning a great deal requires an explanation of durability and competition.

Avoid declaring every intangible worthless or every high return permanent. Write what a buyer would need to recreate, what could be sold independently, and what might disappear if the organization stopped operating.

book = 200 - 120
tangible = book - 50
print("Book and tangible equity per share:", book / 10, tangible / 10)

    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Assets are 150 including 35 goodwill; liabilities are 90 and there are 5 shares. Calculate book and tangible equity per share, then state why neither must equal intrinsic value.
assignment.solution: Book equity is 60, or 12 per share. Tangible equity is 25, or 5 per share. Recoverability, unrecorded business strengths, obligations, and earning power can produce a different economic estimate.

modules.title: Compare businesses on consistent terms
modules.subtitle: Construct a peer comparison with matching claims, normalized earnings, and accounting assumptions.
modules.objective: Construct a peer comparison with matching claims, normalized earnings, and accounting assumptions.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VII. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## A multiple compresses assumptions

A price-to-earnings ratio combines the market value of common equity with earnings attributable to common owners. An enterprise multiple pairs the value of operating claims with an operating measure. Mixing enterprise value with common EPS produces an incoherent comparison.

Cheapness is relative to an economic denominator. Two identical reported multiples can conceal different leverage, cyclicality, accounting policies, reinvestment needs, and customer concentration. Begin with a small comparable set and explain the reasons for inclusion. A large automated ranking does not establish comparability.

Normalize earnings before comparing multiples. Record how taxes, unusual items, minority interests, and diluted shares are treated. A low multiple at peak profit can be more expensive than a higher multiple on depressed but recoverable earnings.

$$
EV=\text{equity market value}+\text{debt}-\text{excess cash}
$$

## A worked example

Alder has equity market value of $120 million, debt of $60 million, and excess cash of $20 million. Enterprise value is $160 million. Normalized EBIT is $20 million, giving EV/EBIT of 8 times. A peer has equity value of $150 million, debt of $10 million, no excess cash, and normalized EBIT of $20 million: also 8 times.

The companies have the same enterprise multiple but different financing risk. Alder's common holders stand behind more net debt. If operating values fall by the same amount, the percentage impact on their smaller residual equity can be larger.

## Explain the residual difference

Build a bridge from reported to comparable figures for each company. Then identify the facts a multiple does not capture: asset quality, business durability, governance, and required reinvestment. A peer's market price is another market observation, not independent proof of intrinsic value.

Use comparables to challenge an estimate. If your conclusion requires a much higher multiple than similarly exposed businesses, explain the difference in economics. Do not import the peer average solely because it creates an attractive upside.
modules.code:
ev = 120 + 60 - 20
print("Enterprise value:", ev)
print("EV / normalized EBIT:", ev / 20)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Company A has equity 90, debt 40, excess cash 10, and normalized EBIT 15. Company B has equity 100, debt 20, no excess cash, and EBIT 12. Compare EV/EBIT and name two reasons the lower ratio may not be the better investment.
assignment.solution: A is 120 / 15 = 8 times; B is 120 / 12 = 10 times. A may have greater cyclicality, weaker asset quality, more financing risk, or greater reinvestment needs. The ratio alone cannot settle value.

modules.title: Special situations and contingent outcomes
modules.subtitle: Analyze a price discrepancy using completion, failure, timing, and funding scenarios.
modules.objective: Analyze a price discrepancy using completion, failure, timing, and funding scenarios.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VII. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## A spread describes a contingent claim

A announced cash transaction, liquidation, or exchange can create a difference between today's price and a possible future receipt. The spread is not free profit. Completion can fail, timing can stretch, and interim financing or liquidity can become expensive.

Start with the actual mechanism that turns the security into cash or another claim. List conditions, required approvals, financing dependencies, and what the holder owns if the event fails. Treat probability estimates as assumptions to be tested, not objective frequencies merely because a spreadsheet accepts them.

A positive expected payoff can coexist with a large loss in an adverse outcome. Position size, correlation among events, and the ability to hold through delays matter separately from the expected value calculation.

$$
p_{break-even}=(P-V_{failure})/(V_{success}-V_{failure})
$$

## A worked example

A fictional target costs $45. A stipulated cash deal pays $50 if completed; estimated standalone value after failure is $32. If the analyst assumes an 80% completion probability, expected terminal proceeds are 0.8 × 50 + 0.2 × 32 = $46.40, before discounting and costs. Expected gain is $1.40, while failure loses $13.

Ignoring timing and costs, the break-even completion probability solves 45 = p × 50 + (1 − p) × 32. It is 13 / 18 = 72.22%. A lower assumed probability produces a negative expected payoff. Longer waiting periods can reduce attractiveness even if the event ultimately completes.

## Write both stories

Describe why completion should occur and what evidence would support failure. Avoid treating management's target date as a certainty. Test the failure value independently; it may have changed since the announcement.

Keep the arithmetic, probability judgment, and risk budget separate. An attractive spread may compensate for a risk the portfolio cannot tolerate. The decision should survive a plausible adverse scenario rather than relying entirely on the most likely outcome.
modules.code:
print("Expected proceeds:", 0.8 * 50 + 0.2 * 32)
print("Break-even probability:", (45 - 32) / (50 - 32))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: An event costs 28, pays 35 on success, and leaves value of 15 on failure. Calculate break-even probability and expected proceeds at a 70% assumed success probability, before timing and costs.
assignment.solution: Break-even probability is (28 − 15) / (35 − 15) = 65%. Expected proceeds are 29, a gain of 1; failure loses 13. Costs, delay, and an overstated failure value could erase the apparent advantage.

exercise.question: Success pays 40, failure 20, and price is 30. Break-even probability before costs is:

exercises.question: Success pays 40, failure 20, and price is 30. Break-even probability before costs is:
A positive expected event payoff establishes:
options: An assumption-dependent average, not guaranteed completion
exercises.explanation: The adverse outcome remains possible and can be much larger than the expected gain.

modules.title: From an estimate to a monitored decision
modules.subtitle: Write an investment memo with an opposing case, price discipline, and explicit review triggers.
modules.objective: Write an investment memo with an opposing case, price discipline, and explicit review triggers.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VII. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Analysis must lead to a revisable decision

A useful memo connects evidence to action. State the security, claim priority, value premise, conservative range, required discount, and source of realization. Then present the strongest opposing case. If the adverse argument is trivial, the research may not yet have confronted the real uncertainty.

Separate business review triggers from price review triggers. A lost customer, covenant change, or unexpected cash drain can alter value. A quotation reaching a target can alter the prospective return without changing the business. Both matter, but they should not be confused.

Position sizing introduces portfolio considerations beyond the security estimate. Several apparently unrelated bargains may depend on the same refinancing market or economic cycle. A discount to value does not eliminate the consequences of concentrated exposure.

$$
\text{Scenario portfolio loss}=\text{position weight}\times\text{position loss}
$$

## A worked example

A researcher estimates weak-case value at $40 per share and requires a 30% discount, producing a maximum purchase price of $28. The stock trades at $26. The memo identifies a customer representing 35% of revenue and a debt maturity in eighteen months as its two major risks.

A stress loss of 40% on the position would cost 2% of portfolio value if the initial position were 5%, assuming other holdings were unchanged. This is a scenario budget, not a bound on possible loss. A larger impairment or correlated losses could be worse.

## Use a repeatable review

Record the dated evidence supporting each assumption, the next expected information release, and the condition requiring reassessment. Compare actual results with the thesis rather than only with the share price. Preserve the original memo so later success does not erase the uncertainties present at purchase.

A sound conclusion can be buy, watch, avoid, or insufficient evidence. No numerical valuation obliges a trade. What matters is whether the claim, price, and evidence together satisfy the stated process.

print("Maximum price:", 40 * 0.70)
print("Scenario portfolio loss (%):", 0.05 * 0.40 * 100)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Write a six-line memo for value 50, price 32, and a required 35% discount. Include a 6% position exposed to a 50% stress loss, one evidence gap, and a review trigger.
assignment.solution: Maximum price is 32.50, so 32 satisfies the numerical rule. Scenario portfolio loss is 3%. A complete memo still needs evidence supporting value, an opposing case, the unresolved fact, and a trigger tied to business or financing developments.

modules.title: The Graham growth heuristic: a separate extension
modules.subtitle: Audit the units and sensitivity of a later growth heuristic without treating it as the 1940 book's valuation method.
modules.objective: Audit the units and sensitivity of a later growth heuristic without treating it as the 1940 book's valuation method.
modules.reading: Course extension · modern valuation and synthesis. These tools and the growth heuristic are not presented as methods from the 1940 text.
modules.content:
## Keep historical layers separate

This optional bridge retains the earlier course's growth worksheet. The expression below is a later heuristic commonly associated with Graham; it is not the organizing valuation method of the 1940 Security Analysis course. The course does not use it to replace analysis of earning power, assets, and creditor protection.

The worksheet combines EPS, an assumed growth input, and a reference-yield scaling factor. Its constants are fixed assumptions rather than a complete economic model. It has no explicit cash-flow forecast, reinvestment schedule, fade of competitive advantage, or probability of failure.

In this expression, growth and yield are entered in percentage points: 5 for 5%, and 4.4 for 4.4%. Mixing decimals with percentage points can create an apparently precise but meaningless answer. The mathematical requirement of a positive yield denominator does not establish that the resulting value is appropriate.

$$
V=EPS(8.5+2g)\frac{4.4}{Y}
$$

## A worked example

With EPS of $4, growth input of 5, and yield input of 4.4, the worksheet gives $74. Raising the yield input to 6 reduces the result to about $54.27. Keeping the original yield but raising growth to 10 produces $114.

These large changes come from a few assumptions, without any explicit modeling of the investment needed to achieve growth. If normalized EPS is actually $3 rather than $4, every result falls by 25%. Sensitivity can overwhelm the supposed discount to the market price.

## Use the worksheet as a critique

Reproduce the calculation, label every input, and explain what the formula leaves out. Compare its conclusion with a separate asset and earning-power analysis. A disagreement is a reason to investigate assumptions, not to average three outputs until the desired answer emerges.

For book study, keep this exercise in the extension unit. Its role is to demonstrate the danger of compressing a complex business into a popular rule of thumb.
modules.code:
eps = 4
growth = 5
for yield_points in [4.4, 6]:
    print("Heuristic value:", round(eps * (8.5 + 2 * growth) * 4.4 / yield_points, 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Use EPS 2, growth input 3, and yield input 4.4, then change yield to 5.5. Explain two economic elements absent from the worksheet.
assignment.solution: Values are 29 and 23.20. The formula does not explicitly model required reinvestment, duration of growth, future dilution, or failure risk. Treat its output as an assumption sensitivity, not an independent valuation conclusion.

modules.title: Modern bridge: earning-power and cash-flow valuation
modules.subtitle: Convert operating value into common equity and test discount-rate assumptions in a transparent modern model.
modules.objective: Convert operating value into common equity and test discount-rate assumptions in a transparent modern model.
modules.reading: Course extension · modern valuation and synthesis. These tools and the growth heuristic are not presented as methods from the 1940 text.
modules.content:
## A modern model should preserve analytical discipline

This extension uses contemporary cash-flow notation to apply the course's emphasis on normalized operations and conservative assumptions. It is not attributed to the 1940 text. Begin by defining the cash flow: to the business before debt financing, or to common owners after financing. Use a discount rate consistent with that claim.

A no-growth operating model can capitalize sustainable cash available before financing at an assumed required return. A growing perpetuity additionally assumes stable growth, a consistent reinvestment policy embedded in cash flow, and a discount rate above growth. Those are strong assumptions.

After estimating operating value, add only excess nonoperating assets and deduct debt and other senior claims not already reflected. Do not deduct debt twice if the modeled cash flow and discount rate already value common equity directly.

$$
EV=FCF_1/(r-g);\quad V_{common}=(EV+Cash-Debt)/N
$$

## A worked example

Alder's sustainable annual cash flow to operating capital is estimated at $15 million. A no-growth perpetuity discounted at 10% gives operating value of $150 million. Add $10 million of excess cash and deduct $40 million of debt: common value is $120 million, or $12 with 10 million shares.

At a 12% required return, operating value falls to $125 million and common value to $9.50 per share. If next year's cash flow is still $15 million but a perpetual 2% growth assumption is introduced at a 10% rate, operating value becomes $187.5 million. The increase is an assumption effect, not a newly discovered asset.

## Test the model's dependencies

Show a grid of sustainable cash flow and required return. If growth is included, explain how investment requirements are funded and why the growth-rate assumption is sustainable. Compare with asset evidence without adding mutually exclusive values.

A model is useful when it makes the decision's dependencies inspectable. Its formula does not reduce uncertainty unless the underlying evidence improves.

for rate in [0.10, 0.12]:
    enterprise = 15 / rate
    print("No-growth equity per share:", (enterprise + 10 - 40) / 10)

modules.title: Capstone: the Alder investment committee
modules.subtitle: Deliver a reconciled valuation memo that combines credit protection, earning power, assets, and price discipline.
modules.objective: Deliver a reconciled valuation memo that combines credit protection, earning power, assets, and price discipline.
modules.reading: Course extension · modern valuation and synthesis. These tools and the growth heuristic are not presented as methods from the 1940 text.
modules.content:
## Your case file

All amounts below are fictional millions except per-share figures. The date is the case decision date; assume all listed information was available then. Alder has 10 million common shares at $6.20. Cash is 30, of which 10 is required for operations. Receivables are 50, inventory 70, and recorded fixed assets 90. Total liabilities are 100, including interest-bearing debt of 60. There is no preferred claim.

Reported EBIT is 24, including a nonrecurring pretax asset-sale gain of 4. Annual interest is 5. Weak-case recurring EBIT is 12. For a separate modern no-growth model, use a stipulated sustainable unlevered cash-flow range of 9–12 and a required return of 10%. These cash flows already reflect operating investment needs and taxes.

For an asset realization scenario, recover cash in full, 80% of receivables, 50% of inventory, and 20% of fixed assets. Deduct all recorded liabilities and incremental closure costs of 8. Assume no additional burn in this immediate-realization scenario; then challenge that assumption.

$$
P_{max}=V_{conservative}(1-M_{required})
$$

## A worked example

Normalized EBIT is 20 and normal interest coverage is 4 times; weak coverage is 2.4 times. NCAV is (30 + 50 + 70 − 100) / 10 = $5 per share. Adjusted realization is (30 + 40 + 35 + 18 − 100 − 8) / 10 = $1.50.

No-growth operating value is 90–120. Add only 20 of excess cash, deduct debt of 60, and divide by 10: common value is $5–8 per share. The other operating liabilities are reflected in this case's stipulated operating cash flows; the asset realization separately deducts all liabilities. Explain that difference in your claims bridge.

At $6.20 the discount to the upper endpoint is 22.5%, but the quote exceeds the lower endpoint. A required 30% discount to the $5 conservative operating estimate implies a maximum price of $3.50. The current quote fails that rule.

## Committee deliverable

Write 600–900 words with a claims map, normalized earnings bridge, three valuation premises, downside case, price decision, and monitoring plan. Cite case facts and clearly label your assumptions. Explain why the three values should not be added or mechanically averaged.

Self-assess five criteria, each from 0 to 4: traceable evidence, correct reconciliations, consistent valuation premises, serious downside analysis, and a revisable decision. A score of 3 means correct with explicit limitations; 4 also explains a plausible alternative. Aim for 15/20 with no zero. The notebook stores your memo; the app grades the numerical final exam separately and does not certify the written work.
modules.code:
print("Normalized coverage:", (24 - 4) / 5)
print("Weak coverage:", 12 / 5)
print("NCAV per share:", (30 + 50 + 70 - 100) / 10)
print("Adjusted realization:", (30 + 50 * .8 + 70 * .5 + 90 * .2 - 100 - 8) / 10)
for cash_flow in [9, 12]:
    print("Operating equity estimate:", (cash_flow / .10 + 20 - 60) / 10)
print("Maximum conservative price:", 5 * .70)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Write the committee memo in your notebook. Then stress the case with two years of cash burn totaling 12 before asset realization, and raise the operating discount rate to 12%. Does either sensitivity support the $6.20 quote under the stipulated 30% rule?
assignment.solution: Ignoring additional timing discount, realization falls from 15 to 3 in total, or $0.30 per share. At 12%, operating equity is (75 + 20 − 60) / 10 to (100 + 20 − 60) / 10 = $3.50–6.00. A 30% discount to $3.50 permits $2.45. Neither sensitivity supports the current quote under the chosen rule. A strong memo also questions the timing, recoveries, and durability of cash flow.

questions.question: Annual cumulative preference is 2, with one year in arrears. Current preference also comes first. How much of a distribution of 7 remains?
questions.explanation: Arrears and current preference total 4, leaving 3 for common under these terms.

questions.question: A bond converts into 30 shares at a stock price of 25. Conversion value is:
questions.explanation: 30 shares × 25 per share = 750 of immediate conversion value.

questions.question: A firm retains 16 and adds 2 of recurring annual profit. Implied incremental return is:
questions.explanation: 2 / 16 = 12.5%, subject to the profit and investment assumptions.

questions.question: Value is 120 across 12 shares; 20 of excess cash repurchases shares at 5. Remaining value per share is:
questions.explanation: Four shares retire; remaining value 100 divided by 8 shares is 12.50.

exams.title: Checkpoint · earnings and asset evidence
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Reported EPS of 9 includes a 4 after-tax isolated gain. Recurring EPS with no other adjustments is:
questions.explanation: Subtract the isolated gain: 9 − 4 = 5.

questions.question: Profit is 18, depreciation 2, and net operating working capital rises 5. Simplified operating cash is:
questions.explanation: 18 + 2 − 5 = 15 before any other adjustments.

questions.question: Current assets 90, all liabilities 55, preferred claims 5, and 6 shares imply NCAV per share of:
questions.explanation: (90 − 55 − 5) / 6 = 5 per common share.

questions.question: Assets 180 include goodwill 40; liabilities are 110. Tangible equity is:
questions.explanation: 180 − 110 − 40 = 30; economic recovery still needs investigation.

exams.title: Checkpoint · price discrepancies and decisions
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: An asset surplus of 18 faces total burn of 5 and incremental costs of 4. Residual before discounting is:
questions.explanation: 18 − 5 − 4 = 9; a timing adjustment may reduce present value further.

questions.question: Enterprise value 144 and normalized EBIT 18 imply which multiple?
questions.explanation: 144 / 18 = 8 times normalized EBIT.

questions.question: A claim costs 18, pays 24 on success and 9 on failure. Break-even probability is:
questions.explanation: (18 − 9) / (24 − 9) = 9 / 15 = 60%, before time and costs.

questions.question: A 3% position suffers a 60% loss, other holdings unchanged. Portfolio loss is:
questions.explanation: 0.03 × 0.60 = 0.018, or 1.8% of starting portfolio value.

exams.title: Security Analysis final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: A researcher requires a 25% discount to a weak-case value of $80. The quote is $64. What follows?
options: Buy because the base case is higher
questions.explanation: $80 × 0.75 = $60; the $64 quote provides only a 20% discount to the chosen conservative estimate.

questions.question: A dataset substitutes a June restatement into a March decision. What must the analyst do?
options: Keep it because it is more accurate
Use the March information set and label the later revision
questions.explanation: A reconstruction must preserve what was knowable in March; the June revision belongs to a later information set.

questions.question: An analyst adds a factory's resale value to the capitalized earnings generated by that factory. What is the main defect?
options: The result uses too few decimal places
All asset values must be zero
questions.explanation: The operating valuation already includes the productive asset; its separate sale proceeds describe another premise.

questions.question: EBIT falls from 84 to 28 while annual interest remains 14. What is weak-case coverage?
questions.explanation: The weak case uses 28 / 14 = 2; the historical 6-times ratio is not the stressed result.

questions.question: A parent owns a subsidiary whose assets realize 100 and whose own creditors are owed 90. Ignoring all other costs, what reaches the parent?
questions.explanation: Only the subsidiary's residual 100 − 90 = 10 is available to the parent in this simplified ownership structure.

questions.question: A borrowing test requires 3-times coverage; EBIT is 75 and existing interest is 18. What incremental interest fits?
questions.explanation: Maximum total interest is 75 / 3 = 25, so additional capacity is 25 − 18 = 7.

questions.question: A security costs 102 and pays a coupon of 5 plus call proceeds of 100 exactly one year later. Its return is:
questions.explanation: Total receipts of 105 less cost of 102 give 3 / 102 = 2.94%, before costs and default effects.

questions.question: Annual preferred dividends are 3 with two unpaid years. If current dividends must also be paid first, how much of an available 11 remains for common?
questions.explanation: Arrears of 6 plus the current 3 absorb 9, leaving 2 under the stipulated distribution terms.

questions.question: A convertible priced at 1,100 delivers 50 shares worth 20 each. What is the premium over conversion value?
questions.explanation: Conversion value is 1,000; the 100 premium divided by 1,000 is 10%.

questions.question: A company retains 20 to earn 1 of incremental annual profit. A comparable requirement is 9%. What is the key concern?
options: Its 5% incremental return is below the requirement
The payout ratio must be negative
questions.explanation: 1 / 20 = 5%, below 9% under the stipulated comparison; assumptions and risk need further review.

questions.question: Equity is worth 60 across 6 shares. Spend 12 repurchasing at 12 per share. What value per remaining share results under unchanged operations?
questions.explanation: Value falls to 48 and shares to 5; 48 / 5 = $9.60, below the initial $10.

questions.question: Reported EPS is 8, including a 3 after-tax disposal gain. No other adjustment is justified. What normalized EPS follows?
questions.explanation: Subtract the nonrecurring gain from reported earnings: 8 − 3 = 5.

questions.question: A cost of 100 is spread over 20 years instead of 10, with zero residual. What happens to annual pretax profit, all else equal?
options: It rises by 5 with no immediate cash improvement
questions.explanation: Depreciation falls from 10 to 5, increasing accounting profit by 5 without an immediate cash-flow change.

questions.question: Recorded unit cost is 5, replacement cost 8, and 100 units are sold. How much does recorded gross profit exceed the replacement-cost comparison?
questions.explanation: The cost difference is 3 per unit across 100 units, giving a 300 profit difference.

questions.question: Net income is 12, depreciation 3, and net operating working capital increases 7. With no other adjustments, operating cash is:
questions.explanation: 12 + 3 − 7 = 8 in the stipulated simplified bridge.

questions.question: Cash is 10, receivables 20 at 75% recovery, inventory 30 at 50%, and total senior claims 25. What adjusted residual remains?
questions.explanation: 10 + 15 + 15 − 25 = 15, before any additional realization costs.

questions.question: A net realization of 22 arrives exactly two years from now. At a stipulated 10% discount rate its present value is approximately:
questions.explanation: 22 / 1.10² = 18.18; timing reduces present value even if the nominal recovery is achieved.

questions.question: A company trades below tangible book but earns persistent losses and owns obsolete machinery. What follows?
options: The losses and asset recoverability can invalidate the apparent floor
questions.explanation: Recorded tangible assets may not realize book amounts, and operating losses can consume the remaining resources.

questions.question: A firm has EV of 180 and peak EBIT of 30, but normalized EBIT is 18. Its normalized EV/EBIT is:
questions.explanation: 180 / 18 = 10 times; the 6-times multiple uses peak earnings and understates the normalized ratio.

questions.question: A claim costs 24, pays 30 on success and 10 on failure. At an assumed 60% success probability, expected proceeds are:
questions.explanation: 0.6 × 30 + 0.4 × 10 = 22, below the price even before costs and discounting.

questions.question: Weak-case value is 60 and the required discount is 40%. The quote is 38. What follows?
options: The maximum price is 36, so the stated rule fails
questions.explanation: 60 × 0.60 = 36; a quote of 38 is above the decision boundary.

questions.question: EPS is 3, growth input 2, and yield input 4.4. What does the stipulated heuristic produce?
questions.explanation: 3 × (8.5 + 4) × 4.4 / 4.4 = 37.5, before considering the heuristic's economic limitations.

questions.question: No-growth operating cash flow is 10 at a 10% rate, with excess cash 5, debt 25, and 10 shares. Common value per share is:
questions.explanation: Operating value is 100; common value is 100 + 5 − 25 = 80, or 8 per share.

questions.question: A revised capstone estimates conservative common value at 7 and requires a 30% discount. The quote is 5.20. Which decision follows the stated rule?
options: Reject at this quote; maximum price is 4.90
questions.explanation: 7 × 0.70 = 4.90, below 5.20. The analysis must retain its decision discipline rather than adjust assumptions to fit price.

title: Quantitative Investment Analysis
description: A complete quantitative learning path from discounting and probability to machine learning, factor risk, and reproducible strategy evaluation.
source: CFA Institute · Quantitative Investment Analysis · Fourth edition

modules.title: Time value of money
modules.subtitle: Put cash flows on a timeline and use a discount rate consistent with their timing and units.
modules.objective: Put cash flows on a timeline and use a discount rate consistent with their timing and units.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 1. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## First draw the timeline

Discounting translates cash flows at different dates into a common date. Specify the currency, payment dates, compounding convention, and whether amounts are nominal or inflation-adjusted. A nominal rate belongs with nominal cash flows; mixing it with real cash flows can count inflation inconsistently.

For one payment, moving forward multiplies by the accumulation factor and moving backward divides by it. Multiple payments must each be discounted from their own date. The discount rate represents an assumed opportunity cost appropriate to the modeled cash flow, not a universal constant.

An ordinary annuity pays at period ends. An annuity due pays at period beginnings, so each payment is one period earlier. A growing perpetuity assumes infinitely many payments growing at a constant rate; its familiar formula requires a discount rate above growth.

$$
PV=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}
$$

## A worked example

A fictional fund owes $110 in one year and $121 in two years. At a 10% annual rate, each payment has present value of $100, so total present value is $200. Simply dividing their sum by 1.10 discounts the second payment from the wrong date.

A perpetuity paying $5 next year with 2% growth and a 7% required return has value 5 / (0.07 − 0.02) = $100. The next-year payment belongs in the numerator. If rate and growth are equal, this finite-value formula is undefined.

## Translate a result into a decision

Check whether the selected rate and the timing assumptions match the actual question. A promised payment and an uncertain business cash flow need different risk analysis even if the arithmetic is identical. For a terminal value, show the share of total value that depends on distant assumptions.

Reproduce the timeline before using a spreadsheet function. A correct function with misdated cash flows gives the wrong economic answer.
modules.code:
cash_flows = [110, 121]
pv = 0
for i in range(len(cash_flows)):
    pv = pv + cash_flows[i] / 1.10 ** (i + 1)
print("Present value:", round(pv, 2))
print("Growing perpetuity:", 5 / (.07 - .02))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Discount payments of 105 and 110.25 at the ends of years one and two using 5%. Then move both payments one year earlier and explain the change.
assignment.solution: The ordinary timeline is worth 200. Moving every payment one year earlier multiplies value by 1.05, giving 210. State that the first shifted payment occurs today.

exercise.question: When is a growing-perpetuity valuation finite and positive?
exercise.explanation: The denominator r − g must be positive.

exercises.question: When is a growing-perpetuity valuation finite and positive?
exercises.explanation: The denominator r − g must be positive.

exercises.question: Two equal payments occur at years one and two. Which procedure is correct?
options: Discount each from its own payment date
exercises.explanation: Each cash flow has a different time to receipt and therefore a different discount factor.

modules.title: Compounding, annuities, NPV, and IRR
modules.subtitle: Compare effective rates and evaluate a project without confusing its return estimate with value added.
modules.objective: Compare effective rates and evaluate a project without confusing its return estimate with value added.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 1. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Compounding conventions change the comparison

A quoted nominal annual rate compounded several times per year is not its effective annual rate. If the nominal rate is j and there are m equal compounding periods, each period earns j/m and the effective annual rate is (1 + j/m)^m − 1. Match the payment frequency to the rate used in an annuity calculation.

Net present value subtracts the initial cost from discounted future receipts. Internal rate of return is a rate making that NPV zero. IRR is useful for conventional cash-flow patterns, but multiple sign changes can produce multiple roots or no economically useful root. Projects of different size or timing can also rank differently by IRR and NPV.

A positive NPV is conditional on the projected cash flows and required return. It is not a promise of profit. Preserve the forecast assumptions and examine how much they can deteriorate before value is lost.

$$
EAR=(1+j/m)^m-1
$$

## A worked example

A nominal 12% annual rate compounded monthly has effective rate (1.01)^12 − 1 = 12.6825%. Treating it as exactly 12% understates annual compounding.

A project costs 100 now and pays 60 at each of the next two year ends. At 10%, NPV is −100 + 60/1.10 + 60/1.10² = 4.13. Its IRR is about 13.07%. The NPV answers how much value is added at the stipulated 10% requirement; IRR supplies the break-even rate.

## Diagnose before solving

Write the sign of every cash flow and identify whether the pattern is conventional. Compare mutually exclusive projects on a common basis appropriate to the decision. Reinvestment assumptions, project life, and capital constraints can matter.

When communicating the result, give both the monetary NPV and the assumptions that produce it. A percentage alone can conceal a small economic benefit or a fragile forecast.
modules.code:
from math import sqrt
print("Effective annual rate (%):", ((1 + .12 / 12) ** 12 - 1) * 100)
print("Project NPV:", round(-100 + 60 / 1.1 + 60 / 1.1 ** 2, 2))
print("Project IRR (%):", ((60 + sqrt(60 ** 2 + 4 * 100 * 60)) / 200 - 1) * 100)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Compute the effective rate for nominal 8% compounded quarterly. Calculate NPV of a cost of 100 followed by 55 at each of two year ends at 5%.
assignment.solution: Effective rate is 1.02⁴ − 1 = 8.2432%. NPV is −100 + 55/1.05 + 55/1.05² ≈ 2.27. The project passes the stipulated NPV rule if its forecasts and rate are appropriate.

modules.title: Return measurement and data organization
modules.subtitle: Build a clean return table and distinguish arithmetic, geometric, and log-return summaries.
modules.objective: Build a clean return table and distinguish arithmetic, geometric, and log-return summaries.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 2. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Define one observation

A dataset needs an observational unit: one asset-day, one company-year, or one transaction. Record identifiers, timestamps, currency, total-return treatment, and missing-value rules. A price return excludes distributions unless they are explicitly included. Split-adjusted prices and raw prices should not be mixed in one series.

Simple return is ending wealth divided by starting wealth minus one. Arithmetic mean summarizes the average one-period observation. Geometric mean is the constant compounded rate matching a sequence's terminal wealth. Log returns add across time for the same asset, but simple returns are generally needed for contemporaneous weighted portfolio returns.

Specify whether returns are decimals or percentage points. A decimal value of 0.02 means 2%. Applying a percentage conversion twice can produce errors much larger than any statistical refinement later in the process.

$$
g=\left(\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1+r_t)\right)^{1/T}-1
$$

## A worked example

A hypothetical investment gains 20% and then loses 20%. Starting wealth of 100 becomes 120 and then 96. The arithmetic mean return is zero, but the two-period compounded return is −4%. The geometric mean is the square root of 0.96 minus one, about −2.02% per period.

The two log returns sum to log(0.96), about −0.04082. Exponentiating that sum and subtracting one returns the −4% total simple return. The transformations agree when their definitions are used consistently.

## Inspect before estimating

Sort observations by date, check duplicate asset-date keys, and distinguish absent observations from genuine zero returns. A market closure is not automatically a zero economic return observation at the frequency required by the model.

Keep an untouched source table and a documented transformation table. Later regression or machine learning cannot recover the intended meaning of data that were incorrectly joined, adjusted, or labeled at ingestion.
modules.code:
from math import sqrt, log
print("Terminal wealth:", 100 * 1.2 * .8)
print("Geometric mean (%):", (sqrt(1.2 * .8) - 1) * 100)
print("Sum of log returns:", log(1.2) + log(.8))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: A series returns +10% and −10%. Calculate terminal wealth from 200, arithmetic mean, and geometric mean. State a rule for missing observations.
assignment.solution: Wealth is 198, arithmetic mean 0%, geometric mean √0.99 − 1 ≈ −0.5013%. Missing observations need an explicit, economically justified treatment; do not automatically replace them with zero.

exercise.question: A +50% return followed by −50% changes wealth of 100 to:
exercise.explanation: 100 × 1.5 × 0.5 = 75; equal percentage gains and losses do not cancel.

exercises.question: A +50% return followed by −50% changes wealth of 100 to:
exercises.explanation: 100 × 1.5 × 0.5 = 75; equal percentage gains and losses do not cancel.

exercises.question: Which return summary matches a sequence's compounded terminal wealth?
exercises.explanation: The geometric mean is the constant per-period rate producing the same wealth over the sequence.

modules.title: Describe distributions before fitting models
modules.subtitle: Calculate dispersion and use distribution shape and visual checks to interrogate an average.
modules.objective: Calculate dispersion and use distribution shape and visual checks to interrogate an average.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 2. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## A mean is only one description

Measures of center summarize location. Dispersion describes how widely observations vary. Skewness concerns asymmetry, while tail behavior concerns extreme outcomes. Two return samples can share a mean and standard deviation yet have very different downside experiences.

Sample variance uses n − 1 when estimating population variance from independent observations with an estimated mean. The sample standard deviation is its square root. A population description of a complete stipulated set uses a different denominator. State which question you are answering.

Use a histogram, time plot, and a simple table of quantiles before imposing a model. A histogram can conceal the order of events; a time plot can reveal changing volatility. An outlier may be a genuine event, a corporate action, or a data error. Investigate its origin before removing it.

$$
s^2=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2/(n-1)
$$

## A worked example

A small sample of percentage-point returns is −2, 0, 2, and 4. The mean is 1. Deviations are −3, −1, 1, and 3; squared deviations sum to 20. Sample variance is 20/3 = 6.6667 squared percentage points, and sample standard deviation is about 2.582 percentage points.

If these four outcomes instead form an equally weighted, fully specified population, variance is 20/4 = 5 and standard deviation is about 2.236. The observations did not change; the estimation question did.

## Avoid cosmetic cleaning

Report how many observations were excluded and why. Winsorization replaces extreme values with boundaries; it changes the distribution and must be disclosed. It may improve stability for a purpose but can also conceal the very downside behavior a risk analysis needs to study.

A useful descriptive report includes count, units, frequency, center, dispersion, missingness, and extreme observations with their dates. That evidence helps determine which later model assumptions are plausible.
modules.code:
from math import sqrt
x = [-2, 0, 2, 4]
mean = sum(x) / len(x)
squared = 0
for v in x:
    squared = squared + (v - mean) ** 2
variance = squared / (len(x) - 1)
print("Mean:", mean)
print("Sample standard deviation:", sqrt(variance))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: For observations 1, 3, and 5, calculate the mean and sample standard deviation. Explain why an isolated observation of 50 should be investigated before deletion.
assignment.solution: Mean is 3; squared deviations sum to 8; sample variance is 4 and standard deviation is 2. The observation 50 could be a genuine tail event or an error, and deleting it changes the risk description.

exercise.explanation: The mean is 4 and squared deviations sum to 8; divide by n − 1 = 2 to obtain 4.

modules.title: Conditional probability and Bayes updates
modules.subtitle: Use a probability tree to update a prior belief without confusing conditional directions.
modules.objective: Use a probability tree to update a prior belief without confusing conditional directions.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 3. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Name the event and the information

An unconditional probability describes an event before the specified evidence. A conditional probability restricts attention to outcomes consistent with that evidence. The probability of a signal given distress is generally different from the probability of distress given a signal.

Use joint probabilities to keep the directions straight. Multiplying a prior probability by a conditional signal probability gives the joint probability of both events. Summing across mutually exclusive states gives the total probability of the signal. Dividing the relevant joint probability by that total produces the posterior.

A base rate matters. Even a fairly accurate warning can generate many false alarms when the event is rare. Posterior accuracy depends on the quality and relevance of both prior frequencies and the signal model.

$$
P(D\mid W)=P(W\mid D)P(D)/P(W)
$$

## A worked example

In a fictional population, 10% of firms enter distress. A warning appears for 80% of distressed firms and 20% of nondistressed firms. Joint distress-and-warning probability is 0.10 × 0.80 = 0.08. Joint no-distress-and-warning probability is 0.90 × 0.20 = 0.18.

Total warning probability is 0.26. Conditional distress probability after a warning is 0.08/0.26 = 30.77%. It is neither the 80% signal sensitivity nor the 10% prior. The warning increases risk substantially while still producing more nondistressed than distressed firms among flagged observations.

## Check transferability

Ask whether the reference population resembles the current universe. A model calibrated on one industry or economic regime may have a different false-positive rate elsewhere. Treat supplied probabilities as assumptions in a case, not as universal characteristics of a financial ratio.

Draw the four cells of the joint table and check that their probabilities sum to one. This simple reconciliation prevents many interpretation errors before more elaborate modeling begins.
modules.code:
joint = .10 * .80
warning = joint + .90 * .20
print("Warning probability:", warning)
print("Distress given warning:", joint / warning)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Prior distress is 20%. A warning occurs for 75% of distressed and 25% of nondistressed firms. Calculate the posterior and explain why it is not 75%.
assignment.solution: Joint distress-warning is 0.15; nondistress-warning is 0.20. Posterior is 0.15/0.35 = 42.86%. The 75% quantity conditions on distress, while the desired posterior conditions on seeing the warning.

exercise.question: If P(A)=0.2 and P(B|A)=0.5, P(A and B) is:
exercise.explanation: The joint probability is the prior multiplied by the conditional probability: 0.2 × 0.5.

exercises.question: If P(A)=0.2 and P(B|A)=0.5, P(A and B) is:
exercises.explanation: The joint probability is the prior multiplied by the conditional probability: 0.2 × 0.5.

exercises.question: Why can a useful warning have many false alarms?
options: The event's base rate may be low
exercises.explanation: A large nondistressed population can generate many warnings even with a moderate false-positive rate.

modules.title: Expected return, covariance, and diversification
modules.subtitle: Combine state-dependent returns and explain how covariance changes portfolio uncertainty.
modules.objective: Combine state-dependent returns and explain how covariance changes portfolio uncertainty.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 3. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Keep states aligned

Expected return is a probability-weighted average across stipulated outcomes. Variance measures squared deviations from that expectation. Covariance measures whether two variables tend to deviate in the same direction in the same states. Pairing observations from different dates can destroy the meaning of that relationship.

Portfolio expected return is the weighted average of component expectations. Portfolio variance also includes cross terms. A weighted average of individual variances alone misses the interaction between assets. Correlation is covariance divided by the product of standard deviations and has no units when both standard deviations are positive.

Diversification depends on imperfect co-movement, not simply the number of tickers. Several securities can share the same business or financing exposure. Estimated correlations can also change in adverse conditions.

$$
\sigma_p^2=w_1^2\sigma_1^2+w_2^2\sigma_2^2+2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2
$$

## A worked example

Two assets have annual standard deviations of 20% and 10%, correlation of 0.25, and equal weights. Variance is 0.5² × 0.20² + 0.5² × 0.10² + 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.20 × 0.10 = 0.015. Volatility is √0.015 = 12.25%.

If expected returns are 8% and 4%, the expected portfolio return is 6%. With perfect positive correlation, volatility would be 15%, the weighted average of the two volatilities. The lower 12.25% result depends on the stated correlation assumption.

## Stress the dependence

Repeat the calculation for higher correlation and explain the economic scenario causing it. Covariance estimates from short samples can be unstable. A risk estimate should show its data window, frequency, and whether observations include stressed conditions.

Expected return and volatility are separate summaries. Neither establishes a guaranteed outcome or a complete description of downside risk, especially for asymmetric payoffs.
modules.code:
from math import sqrt
variance = .5 ** 2 * .2 ** 2 + .5 ** 2 * .1 ** 2 + 2 * .5 * .5 * .25 * .2 * .1
print("Expected return:", .5 * .08 + .5 * .04)
print("Portfolio volatility:", sqrt(variance))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Use equal weights in two assets each with 10% volatility. Calculate portfolio volatility at correlations of zero and one. Explain what independence would add beyond zero correlation.
assignment.solution: At zero correlation, variance is 0.005 and volatility 7.071%. At correlation one, volatility is 10%. Zero correlation means no linear covariance; it does not generally imply full probabilistic independence.

exercise.question: Equal weights in assets with expected returns 10% and 2% give expected portfolio return of:
exercise.explanation: 0.5 × 10% + 0.5 × 2% = 6%; covariance affects risk, not this weighted expectation.

exercises.question: Equal weights in assets with expected returns 10% and 2% give expected portfolio return of:
exercises.explanation: 0.5 × 10% + 0.5 × 2% = 6%; covariance affects risk, not this weighted expectation.

exercises.question: Zero correlation generally implies:
options: No linear covariance, but possible nonlinear dependence
exercises.explanation: Uncorrelated variables can still have nonlinear dependence unless stronger distributional assumptions apply.

modules.title: Probability distributions in finance
modules.subtitle: Choose a distribution consistent with the variable and recognize when a normal model understates tail behavior.
modules.objective: Choose a distribution consistent with the variable and recognize when a normal model understates tail behavior.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 4. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Match the model to the variable

A discrete distribution assigns probabilities to countable outcomes. A continuous distribution describes probability over intervals; its density at a point is not a point probability. Before selecting either, define the variable and its possible range.

A normal model is symmetric and unbounded. It can approximate some return behavior, but it permits values below −100% when used directly for simple returns. A lognormal price is positive because its logarithm is normal. Positive prices do not imply normally distributed simple returns.

The model is an assumption to test against the intended use. Real returns can have heavier tails, asymmetry, and changing volatility. A model that approximates the middle of a distribution may perform poorly for rare-loss decisions.

$$
R=e^{r_{log}}-1
$$

## A worked example

Suppose a stipulated one-day normal return has mean zero and standard deviation 1%. The 99% lower-tail loss threshold is approximately 2.326 standard deviations, or 2.326% of value. On a $100,000 position, that is about $2,326 under the model.

This threshold is not a maximum loss. The model itself assigns 1% probability to a worse daily outcome. If the actual distribution has heavier downside tails, the observed frequency and severity beyond the threshold can exceed the model's predictions.

For a separate positive-price model, let a log return equal −0.10. The simple return is exp(−0.10) − 1, approximately −9.52%, rather than exactly −10%.

## Inspect the consequences

Compare empirical tail quantiles with modeled ones and inspect the time pattern of large moves. A normal fit to pooled observations can disguise periods of very different risk. Stress the model using jumps or a mixture of volatility regimes and describe the resulting change in loss estimates.
modules.code:
from math import exp
print("Normal 99% one-day loss threshold:", 100000 * 2.326 * .01)
print("Simple return from log return:", exp(-.10) - 1)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: At zero mean and 2% daily volatility, calculate the normal 95% loss threshold using z=1.645 on 50,000. Explain why the number is not a worst-case loss.
assignment.solution: The threshold is 50,000 × 1.645 × 0.02 = 1,645. Even the assumed normal distribution assigns 5% probability to a larger loss; model misspecification can further worsen outcomes.

modules.title: Counts, joint models, and simulation logic
modules.subtitle: Use a binomial model for repeated trials and identify the assumptions that financial dependence can violate.
modules.objective: Use a binomial model for repeated trials and identify the assumptions that financial dependence can violate.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 4. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## A count model has structural assumptions

A binomial count describes successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability. Its expected count is np and its variance is np(1 − p). These are consequences of the model, not properties of every observed count.

Financial events can cluster. Defaults can respond to a shared recession; trade outcomes can share a volatility regime. Independence can therefore be a particularly fragile assumption when counting adverse events. A correct binomial calculation can still give a poor risk estimate if its premise is wrong.

Simulation draws from an assumed model to approximate outcomes. It does not discover the correct distribution automatically. A reproducible simulation records its seed, parameters, number of draws, and summary error. More draws reduce Monte Carlo noise but do not remove model error.

$$
P(X\geq1)=1-(1-p)^n
$$

## A worked example

Ten fictional independent loans each have a stipulated 2% default probability over one year. Expected defaults are 10 × 0.02 = 0.2. Probability of at least one default is 1 − 0.98^10 ≈ 18.29%. An expected count below one is compatible with a substantial chance of one or more events.

The binomial variance is 10 × 0.02 × 0.98 = 0.196. If defaults become positively dependent, the marginal expected count can remain 0.2 while the distribution of total losses changes materially. Joint assumptions matter beyond individual probabilities.

## Design a useful experiment

State the quantity being estimated before generating draws: a mean, a quantile, or a conditional loss. Compare a small independent case with an exact calculation to validate the simulator. Then introduce a shared adverse state and observe clustering.

Report both numerical uncertainty and structural uncertainty. A narrow Monte Carlo error bar should not be presented as confidence that the chosen economic model is correct.
modules.code:
n = 10
p = .02
print("Expected defaults:", n * p)
print("At least one default:", 1 - (1 - p) ** n)
print("Binomial variance:", n * p * (1 - p))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: For five independent trials with success probability 10%, calculate expected successes and probability of at least one. Name a condition that makes the binomial model unsuitable.
assignment.solution: Expected count is 0.5 and probability is 1 − 0.9⁵ = 40.951%. Dependence between trials or differing success probabilities violates the standard identical-independent binomial setup.

exercise.question: For 20 independent trials with p=0.05, expected successes are:
exercise.explanation: Expected binomial count is np = 20 × 0.05 = 1.

exercises.question: For 20 independent trials with p=0.05, expected successes are:
exercises.explanation: Expected binomial count is np = 20 × 0.05 = 1.

exercises.question: Increasing simulation draws primarily reduces:
exercises.explanation: More draws improve the approximation to the chosen model, but cannot establish that the model describes reality.

modules.title: Sampling & confidence intervals
modules.subtitle: Estimate sampling uncertainty and interpret a confidence interval without treating it as a posterior probability.
modules.objective: Estimate sampling uncertainty and interpret a confidence interval without treating it as a posterior probability.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 5. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## The estimate changes across samples

A sample mean estimates a population mean. Under independent observations with finite variance, its standard error decreases approximately with the square root of sample size. More rows do not necessarily mean proportionally more information when observations are serially dependent or repeatedly describe the same exposure.

When population variance is unknown, a t interval uses the sample standard deviation and an appropriate t critical value. Small-sample exact coverage requires stronger distributional assumptions than a large-sample approximation. Specify sample size, frequency, and the population the sample is intended to represent.

A frequentist 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. After observing one interval, the usual frequentist statement is not that the fixed mean now has a 95% probability of lying inside it.

$$
\bar{x}\pm t^*s/\sqrt{n}
$$

## A worked example

For 25 independent observations with mean return 1% and sample standard deviation 5%, standard error is 5%/√25 = 1%. Using a supplied 95% t critical value of 2.064, the interval is 1% ± 2.064%, or −1.064% to 3.064%.

The interval includes zero, so this two-sided procedure does not establish a positive population mean at that confidence level. It also permits economically meaningful positive and negative values. Failure to isolate a positive mean is not proof the true mean equals zero.

## Describe the sample's limits

Ask whether selection excluded failed funds, delisted securities, or unsuccessful strategies. A precise interval for a biased sample can be precisely wrong for the intended universe. Document the sampling frame before calculating a standard error.

For dependent returns, use a method that reflects dependence, such as an appropriate block-resampling procedure, and state its additional assumptions. Do not silently use the independent-observation formula because it is convenient.
modules.code:
from math import sqrt
mean = .01
se = .05 / sqrt(25)
print("Standard error:", se)
print("95% interval:", mean - 2.064 * se, mean + 2.064 * se)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: A mean is 2%, sample standard deviation 6%, and n=36. Using a supplied critical value of 2.03, compute an interval and explain the effect of quadrupling independent sample size.
assignment.solution: Standard error is 1%; the interval is −0.03% to 4.03%. Quadrupling independent sample size halves standard error, with other inputs held fixed; it does not automatically repair selection bias.

exercise.question: All else equal, quadrupling independent sample size changes standard error by:
exercise.explanation: Standard error scales as 1 / square root of n.

exercises.question: All else equal, quadrupling independent sample size changes standard error by:
exercises.explanation: Standard error scales as 1 / square root of n.

exercises.question: An interval containing zero establishes:
options: The true mean is exactly zero
The data and procedure do not exclude zero at that confidence level
exercises.explanation: Not excluding zero is different from proving the parameter equals zero.

modules.title: Bootstrap, selection bias, and dependent samples
modules.subtitle: Choose a resampling unit that respects the data and distinguish uncertainty estimation from bias correction.
modules.objective: Choose a resampling unit that respects the data and distinguish uncertainty estimation from bias correction.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 5. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Resample the right object

The ordinary bootstrap repeatedly samples observations with replacement from the observed sample and recalculates an estimator. The variation across estimates approximates sampling uncertainty under suitable conditions. It relies on the observed sample representing the intended data-generating process.

For serially dependent observations, resampling individual days breaks time relationships. A block bootstrap resamples contiguous groups to preserve some local dependence. Block length creates a tradeoff: very short blocks lose dependence; very long blocks provide fewer distinct units of variation.

A bootstrap does not restore missing failed funds or historical firms removed by a survivor-only screen. It reproduces the sample supplied. Selection bias needs a better sampling frame or an explicit identification argument, not merely more resamples.

$$
\hat\theta_b^*=f(\text{resampled blocks})
$$

## A worked example

A return series is 1%, 1%, −1%, −1%, repeated twice. Its overall mean is zero, but adjacent observations tend to occur in same-sign pairs. Four nonoverlapping two-day blocks have means 1%, −1%, 1%, and −1%.

A case resample choosing the first positive block twice and the two negative blocks gives mean zero; choosing three positive blocks and one negative gives mean 0.5%. The point is the resampling unit: entire pairs remain intact. This tiny example illustrates mechanics and does not establish an optimal block length.

## Design the uncertainty report

Record the estimator, eligible observations, block construction, random seed, and resample count. Compare uncertainty under plausible block lengths and explain why the choice matches the dependence horizon. Keep overlapping labels and related entities in mind when defining groups.

A useful report separates sample uncertainty from coverage of the investment universe. Wide intervals indicate imprecision; a systematically selected universe can create bias even when intervals are narrow.
modules.code:
blocks = [[.01, .01], [-.01, -.01], [.01, .01], [-.01, -.01]]
selection = [0, 0, 2, 3]
total = 0
count = 0
for i in selection:
    for value in blocks[i]:
        total = total + value
        count = count + 1
print("Illustrative block-resample mean:", total / count)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the valuation or statistical claim.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Explain how you would estimate uncertainty for monthly returns from funds that share a manager and include only surviving funds. Identify one dependence issue and one selection issue.
assignment.solution: Shared management may require grouping related funds or otherwise modeling cross-sectional dependence. Survivor-only inclusion omits failed funds and requires reconstruction of the historical universe; resampling survivors cannot fix that omission.

exercise.explanation: Independent day draws break neighboring relationships that may determine estimator uncertainty.

exercises.question: Resampling individual days from a serially dependent series can:
exercises.explanation: Independent day draws break neighboring relationships that may determine estimator uncertainty.

The number of computed resample means
exercises.explanation: More resamples cannot add excluded observations or correct the sampling frame by themselves.
